VALEDICTORY REMARKS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, we have come to the close of this 204*' 
Session of Rajya Sabha which commenced on Friday, the 25th February with Presidents' 
Address to the Members of both the Houses. As usual, this has been a long Session 
with interregnum from 25* March to 18th April when the Department-related Standing 
Committees worked hard to examine the Demands for Grants of various Ministries 
and Departments. 
Being the Budget Session, the prime bu siness of the House related to the 
Railway Budget and the General Budget of the Union. The House also had this 
time the opportunity to have a discussion on the Budgets of Goa and Bihar as 
these States are under President's Rule. Besides the Budget, the House also 
transacted substantial legislative and other business. 
During the Session, 26 Bills were considered and passed or returned. Apart 
from the Money Bills, the other notable Bills passed by the House were the 
Patents (Amendment) Bill, 2005, the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 
the University of Allahabad Bill, 2004, the Private Security Agencies (Regulation) Bill, 
2005, the Special Economic Zones Bill, 2005 and the most important of all, the 
Right to Information Bill, 2005. The passing of these Bills would provide 
improved policy and statutor y framework for economic growth as well as better 
governance for the people. 
Hon. Members, it has always been my sanguine hope and wish, as also 
my very sincere endeavour that t he conduct of the business and House 
should purposefully address the problems of the people. I have, therefore, 
always actively encouraged and lent full support to discussion and debate on 
important issues and challenges of  overcoming underdevelopment and 
promoting people's welfare. I am happy that in this 
343 

RAJYA SABHA [13 May, 2005] 
Session, we not only had the opportunity to have discussion on the working of eight Ministries, 
but also hold valuable discussion on important and wide ranging subjects such as 
problems faced by farmers, relief and rehabilitation to Tsunami victims, need for 
extension of mid-day meal scheme, problem of school drop-outs, promotion of Urdu 
language and reforms in the system of criminal justice. The enlightened discussion and 
illuminating debates of high standards of quality as well as content took place on these 
occasions, thus further enhancing the dignity and stature of this House of Elders. 
Hon. Members, it is, however, a matter of regret that during the last so many days we 
missed the participation by our friends on my left. In the absence of participation by the 
Opposition, the conduct of business in the House lacks the flavour that comes only with active 
and vibrant participation by Members, belonging to all political groups and parties. All of us 
here have the obligation, as also the responsibility to fulfil the aspirations and expectations 
of the people and to promote their welfare through constructive and purposeful discussion and 
debate on all issues relevant to addressing the problems of the people. We, therefore, 
need to do serious introspection as to how we together should ensure effective 
functioning of the House with full and complete participation by all sections. I urge you all 
to address these issues with a sense of urgency, seriousness and shared concern. 
Hon. Members, I hope the heat of the summer would get over soon; and with the pleasant 
and cool showers of mutual understanding and constructive cooperation, when we meet in the 
Monsoon Session of the Parliament, all of us will be working together with a sense of shared 
responsibility and joint commitment to strengthen our parliamentary democracy. Hon. Members, 
I take this opportunity to express my gratitude to the Leader of the House, the Leader of the 
Opposition, leaders of various parties and groups, and all the Members for their kind co-
operation. I also thank the Deputy Chairman, Members of the Panel of Vice-Chairmen and the 
staff of the Secretariat for their help and co-operatbn. Before we adjourn, may I extend to all of 
you my warm greetings and good wishes for the coming months? 
THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH); Mr. Chairman, Sir, I seek your 
permission to begin by expressing my very sincere thanks to you personally, and to the hon. 
Deputy Chairman for the grace and wisdom 
344 

[13 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
with which both of you have conducted the proceedings of this House. We are all 
grateful to you, Sir, for the sense of fairness and fair play with which you dealt with 
each Member of this august House. Sir, this has been a very important Session 
of Parliament. Not only did we discuss the Union and Railway Budgets, but also 
we passed over a dozen Bills including the Patents (Amendment) Bill, the Right to 
Information Bill, the Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Bill, the 
Weapons of Mass Destruction and their Delivery Systems (Prohibition of Unlawful 
Activities) Bill, and the Special Economic Zone Bill. Nine important Bills were 
introduced in the House including the Manipur University Bill and the Disaster 
Management Bill. Sir, we also found time for Short Duration Discussions on many 
matters of national importance such as instances of suicide by farmers, the situation 
arising out of the tsunami disaster last December and the measures taken to deal 
with it, the reform of our criminal justice system and work of the newly-
constituted North-East Council. The House also heard a wide range of important 
policy statements made, and I had the privilege of placing before the House a 
comprehensive statement on my meetings with important foreign dignitaries, 
particularly the Prime Minister of China and the President of Pakistan. Sir, by 
any standards of parliamentary work this is a commendable business. I 
sincerely wish I could have stopped here after recording my appreciation of the 
proceedings. However, Mr. Chairman, Sir, once again, we end the session with a 
sense of regret and concern. You have expressed your noble sentiments and I wish to 
associate myself fully with those sentiments. Sir, at the end of the last session, I 
had expressed my sadness at the manner in which the proceedings of the House 
could not take place. This time, Sir, once again, I stand before you with a profound 
sense of sadness. I believe I would not be expressing the mood of the nation if I 
did not express my regret at the boyco tt of the proceedings of the House by 
many Members of the Opposition. Sir,  the people of India have reposed their 
faith and trust in us and have sent us here to project and protect their interests, 
to canvass and convey their concerns, to influence and shape Government policy 
for the benefit of our people. We are here, Sir, to voice the views of the people and 
not to ignore them by staying away and giving no expression to the concerns of 
our people. Sir, I wish to reiterate that the House is the proper forum to debate and 
discuss any subjects. Our Government stands willing to discuss on the floor of 
the House all issues and any concerns that Members of the House may have in 
mind and regardless of the side to which they may 
345 

RAJYA SABHA [13 May, 2005] 
belong. I, therefore, hope that the next session will be conducted with the full 
participation of the Opposition so that we are able to make better use of our time 
serving the interest of our people. There is an obligation on both the Government 
and the Opposition, to play their respective roles in this august House so that the 
system of checks and ba lances envisaged by our founding fathers works 
effectively and efficiently for the common benefit of our country. I, therefore, 
reiterate my appeal to the Members of the Opposition to return to Parliament 
so that we can resume the normal tenor of Parliamentary work, in accordance 
with the aspirations of the people we all represent. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, with these words, I, once again, thank you for your 
guidance. I also place on record our thanks to the hon. Deputy Chairman, the hon. 
Leader of the Opposition, even though he is absent, the Secretary General and his 
staff for all their good work. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Thank you, Mr. Prime Minister. Now, before we adjourn the 
House sine die, we will have the national Song. 
(The National Song, "Vande Mataram", was then played) MR. 
CHAIRMAN: The House is adjourned sine die.

RAJYA SABHA

OBITUARY   REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Shyam Lal, a former Member of this House; Shri Sunil 
Dutt, a sitting Member of Lok Sabha and Union Minister of Youth Affairs and 
Sports; Shri Sunder Singh Bhandari, Shri Bipinpal Das, Shri Bal Ram Singh 
Yadava and Dr. Rafiq Zakaria, former Members and Dr. Biplab Dasgupta,  a 
sitting Member of this House. 
Shri Shyam Lal, passed away on the 14 th March, 2005, at the age of 
66 years. Born at village Kusumhi in Jau npur district of Uttar Pradesh in July, 
1939. Shri Shyam Lai had his educ ation at SGRI College, Jaunpur and 
Railway Technical Institute, Lucknow. A political and social worker, Shri Shyam 
Lal was associated with various social we lfare and educational institutions. He 
was President of the Akhil Bharatiya Sh oshit Kalyan Parishad. Shri Shyam Lal 
also had a few publications to his credit. The legislative career of Shri Shyam 
Lal started with the membership of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council, 
where he was a member from May, 1984 to May, 1990. 
Shri Shyam Lal represented the State of Uttar Pradesh in this House from 
February, 2001 to November, 2002. In the passing away of Shri Shyam Lai, 
the country has lost a noted social worker. 
Shri Sunil Dutt passed away on the 25th May, 2005 at the age of 76 years. 
Born at Khurd village of Jhelum district  now in Pakistan, in June, 1929, Shri 
Dutt had his education at Jai Hind College, Mumbai. 
A multifaceted personality, Shri Dutt was a film artist and political and 
social worker. Shri Dutt acted in nearly 100 films and also directed and 
produced a few films. Many of his film s were screened at several International 
Film Festivals. Shri Dutt was also asso ciated with various social welfare and 
cultural organizations. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2005] 
Shri Dutt was devoted to serve the cancer patients. He made a film on 
cancer and its cure and donated the profit  earned through this film to the Tata 
Memorial Hospital. He established the Nargis Dutt Memorial Foundation in 
U.S.A., U.K., Canada, Germany and Ho lland and helped different charitable 
hospitals in the country devoted to the tr eatment of cancer by ensuring supply 
of equipment worth three million US Dollars. 
Shri Dutt actively involved himself in raising funds for relief and 
rehabilitation of victims of natural calamities and communal violence. He 
himself also used to contribute generously for national and social causes. Shri 
Dutt cared for the welfare of slum dwellers and fought for providing basic 
amenities to the people living in  slums. He undertook many padyatras for 
promoting peace and communal harmony. He also organized a few 
international conferences on drug abus e and visited different parts of the 
country to promote awareness on HIV/AIDS. 
The long and illustrious political career of Shri-Dutt commenced when 
he was first elected to the Eighth Lok Sabha. He was also elected to the Ninth, 
Tenth, Thirteenth and Fourte enth Lok Sabha. He served as the Union Minister 
of Youth Affairs and Sports from May, 2004 till his sad demise. Shri Dutt also 
had the distinction of serving as Sheriff of Mumbai from 1981 to 1982. 
A recipient of Padmashree Award in 1968, Shri Dutt received several 
awards in recognition of his valuable contributions in the field of cancer 
treatment, promoting peace and communal harmony, fight against violence and 
terrorism and service to the film industry. 
Shri Sunil Dutt always stood for probity in public life. He has left 
behind an indelible mark because of his deep humanism and fight for 
communal harmony and social cohesion. I can never forget the moment when 
along with heart-rending news of his s ad demise, I received a letter from him 
which he had written just a day before his death. In response to the media 
reporting about my humble contribution for the marriage of the daughter of a 
widow of a person whose husband had donated all his organs before his death, 
Shri Dutt had enclosed with his letter a cheque of Rs. 25,ooo/-. Even this last 
act of his was one of sublime kindness; indeed throughout his life he was 
dedicated to the service of the needy and the poor. 
In the passing away of Shri Sunil Dutt, the country has lost an eminent 
parliamentarian, a brilliant actor and a great humanist. 
2 

[25 Juiy, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Shri Sunder Singh Bhandari passed away on the 22 June, 2005. at 
the age of 85 years. Born at Udaipu r in Rajasthan, Shri Bhandari had his 
education at Sirohi, Udaipur and Kanpur. 
An advocate and a teacher by profession, Shri Bhandari was an 
active social and political worker. He was one of the founder members of the 
Bharatiya Janata Party and the erstwhile Bharatiya Jana Sangh. Shri Bhandari 
served as General Secretary of the B haratiya Jana Sangh, Rajasthan, from 
1951 to 1964 and as its All India General Secretary from 1967 to 1977. He was 
also a senior Vice-President of the Bharatiya Janata Party. Shri Bhandari 
represented the State of Rajasthan in this House for two terms from April, 1966 
to April, 1972 and again from July, 1992 to April, 1998. He also represented 
the State of Uttar Pradesh in this House from April, 1976 to April, 1982. He was 
Chairman of the Committee on Petitions from 1992 to 1994 and of the 
Standing Committee on Transport and Tourism from 1996 to 1997. Shri 
Bhandari was also a member of the Indian Delegation to the Inter 
Parliamentary Union Meeting at Lisbon , Portugal in the year 1978. Shri 
Bhandari also had the distinction of servi ng as Governor of t he States of Bihar 
and Gujarat. The passing away of Shri Sunder Singh Bhandari, the country has 
lost an eminent parliamentarian and an able administrator. 
Shri Bipinpal Das passed away on the 3 rd July, 2005, at the age of 82 
years. 
Born at Guwanati in February, 1923,  Shri Das had his education at 
Cotton College, Guwahati, Presidenc y College, Kolkata and the Banaras 
Hindu University. 
An educationist, Shri Das took part in the .freedom struggle in 1942 
and courted imprisonment. He was also actively associated with various 
struggles of the people of Manipur in la te forties and early fifties and visited 
Nagaland as a member of the goodwill mission during the period of political 
unrest there in 1953. 
Having specialization in Pure Physi cs, Shri Das started his career as 
a lecturer of Physics in the Ashutosh Coll ege, Kolkata in 1945. He was also a- 
lecturer in the Darrang College of Tezpur from 1947 to 1950 and served as 
Principal and Frofessor of that college from 1959 to 1968. 
Shri Bipinpal Das represented the State of Assam in this House for 
two consecutive terms from    April, 1970 to April, 1976 and again from April, 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2005]  
1976 to April, 1982. He was Chief Whip of the Congress Party in Rajya Sabha 
from 1977 to 1979. He was also Chairman of the Committee on Petitions, 
Rajya Sabha from 1979 to 1982. Shri Das was also elected to the Eighth Lok 
Sabha. Shri Das served as Union Deputy Mi nister in the Ministry of External 
Affairs from 1974 to 1977. 
A widely travelled person, Shri Das was member of various Indian 
delegations and goodwill missions to abr oad and represented the country in 
several international events. He was a me mber of the Indian delegation to the 
United Nations General Assembly Session in 1971 and again attended 30 th 
Session of the U.N. in the year 1975. 
In the passing away of Shri Bipinpal Das, the country has lost a 
distinguished parliamentarian, a noted educationist and an able administrator. 
Shri Bal Ram Singh Yadava passed away on the 4th July, 2005 at the 
age of 67 years under tragic cirumstanc es. Born at village Kharagpur Sarraiya 
in Etawah District of Uttar Pradesh in April, 1939, Shri Yadava had his 
education at Etawah and Lucknow. An  advocate and an agriculturist by 
profession, Shri Yadava was an active social and political worker. He was 
keenly associated with the welfare and uplift of weaker and vulnerable sections 
of the society. He was associated with various welfare organizations and also 
stood for development of the rural areas. He was Chairman of the Uttar 
Pradesh Mandi Parishad and Uttar Pradesh Agro Industrial Corporation Limited 
from 1980 to 1982. He also served as Senior Deputy Chairman of the Uttar 
Pradesh Youth Welfare Board. 
The long and distinguished political ca reer of Shri Yadava started with 
the membership of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly from 1969 to 1974 
and again from 1980 to 1984. He served as Deputy Minister in the Government 
of Uttar Pradesh from 1969 to 1970 and as Cabinet Minister from 1971 to 1973 
and again from 1980 to 1984. Shri Yadava represented the State of Uttar 
Pradesh in this House from April, 1990 to  April, 1996. He was also elected to 
the Eighth, Twelfth and Thirteenth Lok Sabha. Shri Yadava also served as 
Union Minister of State of the Ministry of Mines from 1991 to 1995 and of the 
Ministry of Planning and Programme Implementation from 1995 to 1996. A 
widely travelled person, Shri Yadava wa s member of the Indian Parliamentary 
Delegation to Yugoslavia in the year 1986 and to Turkey in the years 1992 and 
1998. 
In the passing away of Shri Bal Ram Singh Yadava, the country has 
lost a distinguished parliamentarian and a devoted social worker. 
4 

[25 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Dr. Rafiq Zakaria, a former Member of this House, passed away on 
9lh July, 2005 at the age of 86 years.' Born at Sopara in Thane District of 
Maharashtra in April, 1920, Dr. Zaka ria had his education at the Bombay 
University, London University and Inns of Court, London. A Chancellor's Gold 
Medalist of the University of Bombay, Dr. Zakaria received his Ph.D. from the 
University of London. He was also called to the Bar from Lincoln's Inn. A 
lawyer and a journalist, Dr. Zakaria was associated with various social welfare 
and educational institutions in various capacities. He was Chancellor of the 
Jamia Urdu, Aligarh and helped in setting up of several educational institutions 
in Maharashtra. He was founder President of the Maulana Azad Educational 
Trust that manages various educationa l institutions at Aurangabad in 
Maharashtra. 
An outstanding scholar and historian, Dr. Zakaria was a prolific writer 
on Indian Affairs, Islam and British Imperialism. He had several publications to 
his credit. The legislative career of Dr. Zakaria, which spanned over two 
decades, started with the membership of  Maharashtra Legislative Council from 
i960 to 1962. Thereafter, he was elected to the Maharashtra Legislative 
Assembly in 1962 and remained a member of that Assembly till 1978. He 
served as Deputy Minister in the Gove rnment of Maharashtra from 1962 to 
1964 and as Cabinet Minister from 196 4 to 1977 and held the portfolios of 
Revenue, Public Health, Urban Development, Tourism and Protocol. Dr. 
Zakaria represented the State of Maharashtra in this House from April, 1978 to 
April, 1984. He was also nominated to  the Panel of Vice-Chairmen of Rajya 
Sabha for the years 1980-81, 1981-82 an d 1982-83. Dr. Zakaria represented 
India at the United Nations General Assembly. He also led the Family Planning 
Delegation of the Government of India to  the United States of America in the 
year 1969. He was special invitee to t he World of Islam Festival in London in 
the year 1976. In the passing away of Dr. Rafiq Zakaria, the country has lost 
an able parliamentarian, an eminent schol ar of Islamic history and a prolific 
writer. 
Dr. Biplab Dasgupta passed away on the 17th July, 2005 at the age of 
67 years following prolonged illness. 
Born at Kolkata in December, 1938,  Shri Dasgupta had his education 
at College of Arts and College of Law, University of Kolkata, London School of 
Economics and Institute of Computer Science, University of London. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2005]  
An Economist, Dr. Dasgupta started his professional career as a 
lecturer in Statistics in the Goldsmith' s College of the University of London, 
from 1965 to 1966; lecturer in Econom ics and Statistics in the University 
School of Oriental and African Studies , London, from 1966 to 1972; Reader 
and Fellow in Economics and Statistics in the Institute of Development Studies 
of the University of Sussex, from 19 72 to 1980; and was also Professor of 
Economics,   University  of    Kolkata    from    1980  to 1998. 
He was President of the Governing Body of the South Calcutta Law 
College, Kolkata since 1984 and Director of the Centre for Urban Economic 
Studies, University of Kolkata, from 1980 to 1987 and again from 1992 to 1998. 
He also held temporary assignments as Consultant and Expert with 
the United Nations for varying time periods at its various organizations namely, 
FAO, ILO, UNRISD, UNEP and UNESCO. 
Dr. Dasgupta was Convener of the U.K. Committee for Civil Liberties 
in India from 1975 to 1977. He was also Chairman of the Committee on 
Perspective Plan for Calcutta, Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority 
and Committee on Animal Husbandry, Government of West Bengal from 1985 
to 1987. 
A prolific writer, Dr. Dasgupta had several publications to his credit. 
He was also editor of the Bengali literary monthly 'Nandan'. 
Dr. Dasgupta represented the State of  West Bengal in this House for 
two consecutive terms from April, 1994 to April, 2000 and again from April, 
2000 till he breathed his last. Dr. Das gupta was Deputy Leader of C.P.I.(M) 
Party, in Rajya Sabha from 1994 to 2004. He was also elected to the Ninth Lok 
Sabha in the year 1989. Dr. Dasgupta contributed significantly towards the 
proceedings of the House especially relating to economic and financial matters. 
Dr. Dasgupta attended many internat ional seminars, conferences and 
workshops. He was member of the ILO Employment Mission to Afghanistan in 
the year 1978. 
In the passing away of Dr. Dasgupta the country has lost an eminent 
economist, and a distinguished parliamentarian. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Shyam Lai, Shri Sunil 
Dutt, Shri Sunder Singh Bhandari,   Shri Bipinpal Das, Shri Bal Ram Singh 
6

REFERENCES BY THE CHAIR 
Reference to victims  of bomb blasts in London 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, we in India were shocked and 
deeply saddened when we learnt of the terrorist bomb blasts in London on the 
7th of July, 2005, which resulted in the loss of so many innocent lives and 
injury to many more. We condemn the terrorist acts and express our sympathy 
and solidarity with the people of the UK in their hour of grief. 
India having been a victim of terrorism for more than two decades, 
shares with deep empathy, the anguish and pain of the people of the UK at 
these heinous acts. Such terrorist attacks underline the fact that open and 
democratic societies like our own are especially vulnerable and, therefore, 
need to strengthen cooperation, in a coordinated and concerted manner in 
order to free the world of this scourge. 
Reference to terrorist attack In Sharm-el-Sheikh, Egypt 
MR. CHAIRMAN: We are deeply shocked, appalled and grieved by 
the horrendous terrorist a ttacks on civilians in Sha rm-el-Sheikh, Egypt in the 
early hours of Friday, the 23 rd of July, 2005 on the auspicious occasion of the 
National Day of the Arab Republic of Egypt, resulting in large scale civilian 
deaths and injury. 
The Indian Parliament strongly condemns this ruthless attack on 
innocent civilians by terrorists and offers its sincere condolences to the 
bereaved families, and to the Government of the Arab Republic of Egypt. 
Terrorism which threatens peace and dialogue cannot be justified under any 
guise or motivation. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the memory of those who lost their lives in these tragedies. 
7

changes in forecasts on global climat e, geo-political developments in oil

from 5% to nil and in other petroleum products from 15-20% to 10%.

prices of sensitive products, namely PDS Kerosene, Domestic LPG, Petrol and

AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in view of the fast depleting and drying oil reserves, not only in

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) Given the in creasing gap between demand and 
domestic availability of cr ude oil, besides taking measures to accelerate 
exploratory activities for enhancing domestic oil and gas production, it has 
become essential for our energy security to step up efforts overseas in search of 
equity oil and gas. Towards this end, and in keeping with the objecives of the 
National common Minimum Programme, ONGC, videsh Ltd. (OVL) as well as 
other National Oil Companies (NOCs) such as Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (IOC), 
Oil India Ltd. (OIL) and Gail (India) Ltd. (GAIL) have been pursuing the 
acquisition of equity oil as well as oil and gas exploration acreages and 
producing properties abroad. 
Looking into the vast possibilities of forging alliances with Chinese oil 
companies, the NOCs of India and China keep in touch with each other on a case-
to-case basis. A joint Task Force of the Ministries of External Affairs and 
Petroleum and Natural Gas has been established to examine the prospects for 
Sino-lndian cooperation in the hydrocarbon sector.

country, out of the total capacity addition of 14,393 MW targeted for the 10th 
Five Year Plan (2002—07), the hydro capacity so far added/ commissioned is

10th Plan is about 10,044 MW, including 4,495 MW already achieved. 
64 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In adition to the possibilities of generating nuclear energy from natural and 
enriched uranium, much of which is and will continue to be imported, India has 
vast reserves of thorium. With a view to harnessing the huge potential of 
thorium for electricity generation, Department of Atomic Energy is pursuing a 
three-stage nuclear power programme. The three stages of the programme have 
to be gone through sequentially. The first stage has reached a status of 
commercial maturity. There are 15 nuclear power reactors totaling a capacity 
of 3,310 MW in the country. Construction is also going on in full sowing for 
seting up 7 nuclear power reactors totaling 3,420 MW which will be completed 
in the next three years. We have entered the second sage with the 
commencement of a 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor in the year 2003. 
The third stage of the programme will be launched once we have reached a 
sizeable capacity in the second stage. 
The estimated potential of renewable energy such as wind, small hydro and 
bio-mass is about 80,000 MW in the country. The aim is to deploy ar ound 
3,000 MW capacity from renewables durign the 10th Plan period, comprising 
around 5% from wind (1,500 MW), 2% from small hydro-power (600 MW) and 
3% from bio-energy (900 MW). During the first 3 years of the 10th Plan (2002-
05), 2,643 MW of additional installed power capacity has been commissioned. 
The Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources have prepared on Outline 
Plan for providng energy security to villages through the deployment of bio-energy 
and small hydro technologies. These includ bio-gas plants, bio-mass gasifiers 
and bio-fuels supported by fast-growing energy plantations for woood, 
oilseeds, etc. with the aim of providing to total energy requirments of 
cooking, lighting and motive power, with the full participation of the village 
community, including women, 24 Test Projects on rural energy security have been 
taken up in remote unelectrified villages in 3 States, with a view to demonstrating 
their technical feasibility, providing operational experience, mobilizing local 
communities and firming up institutional arrangements. One such project in 
madhya Pradesh has ben commissioned. The projects are being implemented by 
Gram Panchayats with facilitation by the Zila Parishads, the Forest Departments

Protection of Sub-soil Water 
*34. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that salinisation of sub-soil water is taking 
place in the coastal region and even in interior areas; 
(b) whether Government have assessed the impact of this salinisation of sub-
soil water in the country; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken/proposed to be taken by Government to protect sub-soil 
water? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (d) Studies carried out by the Central Ground Water Board 
(CGWB) and the State Ground Water Departments have indicated salinisation of 
ground water in some parts of the States of Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Gujarat, 
Karnataka, Maharashtra, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Union Teritory 
of Pondicherry. 
Details of State-wise impact of this salinisation is as follows:— 
Andhra Pradesh: Salinity in ground water has been noticed in parts 
of coastal districts fo East Godavari, West Godavari, Prakasam, 
Visakhapatnam, Gunturand Krishna. Sa linity in these areas has its 
genesis to the inherent marine deposition and is not due to sea water 
intrustion. 
Goa: Low lying estuarine regions of various west flowing rivers in the 
State are affected by salinity ingress due to tidal inflow. 
Gujarat: Due to progressive sea water intrusion, the quality of 
ground water is steadily deteriorating in coastal tracts of Kachchh and 
Saurashtra. 
Karnataka: Three districts viz. Uttara Kannanda, Udupi and 
Dakshina Kannada are affected by the problem of salinity ingress in 
ground water due to tidal inflow along the backwater channels. 
Kerala: Salinity of ground water in shallow aquifer has been noticed in 
small pockets in Chellanam and Parur areas of Ernakulam district 
66 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and Azhikkode area of Trichur district. Salinity in these areas is due to the 
influence of tidal waters. In deeper aquifers, the brackishness in the 
formation water is mainly due to leaching of salts from the aquifer 
materials. 
Maharashtra: instances of salinisation of sub-soil water have been 
reported in localized pockets of co astal districts of Thane, Mumbai, 
Raigarh, Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg. 
Orissa: The extreme southern portion of the coastal sedimentary tract 
indicates a marginal quality of water and the salinity increases towards 
Puri. Southwest of Chilka, quality of formation water is marginal to 
saline with a fresh water zone along the top. In and around Puri, 
brackish water is seen sandwiched between the fresh water zones. Salinity 
problem in these areas is inherent and not due to sea water intrusion. 
Tamil Nadu: Salinisation of ground water due to ingrees of sea water, 
caused by excessive withdrawals of ground water from coastal aquifers has 
been observed in parts of Minjur block, Thiruvallur district and near Kottam, 
Radhapuram block in Tirunelveli district. 
West Bengal: Problem of inland salinity has been observed in parts 
of Haldia area of East Medinipur district. No saline water ingress has been 
noticed in the area. 
Pondicherry: Sea water intrusion in coastal aquifers has been 
reported in parts of Pondicherry region of Union Territory of 
Pondicherry. 
'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments concerned to take steps to protect sub-soil water. The 
steps taken/proposed to be taken by the State Government concerned/Union 
Government in this regard are as follows:— 
Andhra Pradesh: Under Andhra Pradesh Water, Land & Trees Act, 
2002, construction of new wells has been banned in coastal areas in order 
to prevent upconing of saline ground water from deeper aquifers. No new 
electric connections are given to lift ground water in these areas. Research 
& Development programme on injection of fresh water during floods in 
the river and canals has shown positive results. 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Goa: Construction of marginal bunds along the bank of rivers in 
estuarine region to arrest the inundation by saline water during high tide in 
low lying areas and construction of bandharas/barrages across the rivers to 
stop the ingress saline water to deep inland has been undertaken by 
Government of Goa. 
Gujarat: Government of Gujarat had constituted two High Level 
Committees to study the salinity problem of Saurashtra and Kachchh regions 
and to suggest remedial measures thereof. The Committees have 
recommended various remedial measures like construction of tidal 
regulators, bandharas, recharge trenches, recharge wells, recharge 
reservoirs, spreading channels etc. Construction of such works has been 
taken by the Government of Gujarat. 
Karnataka: State Government in coordination with the Zila 
Panchayats is undertaking construction of tidal regulators across the 
rivers and rivulets to avoid saline ingress through the rivers during summer 
months. 
Kerala: State Government is constructing tidal regulators and check 
dams across the backwater channels to prevent movement of tidal waters 
inland. 
Maharashtra: In Kelve Mahim area of Thane district, Sweetwater zone 
area has been demarcated. Sinking of new wells and energisation of pump sets 
on existing wells have been restricted to avoid sea water intrusion due 
to heavy pumping. 
Orissa: Under the Central Sector Scheme of 'Study of Recharge to 
Ground Water' implemented during the IX Plan, construction of tidal 
regulators and desilting of creeks was taken up in Bhadrak, Kendrapara 
and Puri districts of Orissa to arrest saline water intrusion. 
Tamil Nadu: Withdrawal of ground from Minjur well field has been 
stopped. Obtaining a license for sinking of wells and energizing them with 
pump (>1 HP) has been made mandatory in the area falling under 
jurisdiction of Chennai Metropolitan Development Area. Installation of 
rain water harvesting has been made mandatory for all buildings in Tamil 
Nadu. Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board has 
carried out pilot study on the possibility of arresting sea water thr ough 
injection of fresh water into the aquifer through tubewells, which showed 
improvement of ground water quality. 
68 

 
[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
West Bengal: The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has 
notified Haldia area of East Medinipur district of West Bengal for the 
purpose of regulation and control of ground water management and 
development to check sea water intrusion. 
Pondicherry: The Pondicherry Government has constituted the 
Pondicherry Ground Water Authority to control and regulate ground water 
development. Extraction of ground water for industrial and irrigation 
uses from wells within 6 km of the coastline has been banned. Installation 
of rain water harvesting has been made mandatory for all buildings.

Measures to Control Inflation 
148. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) Whether it is a fact that Government propose to work out certain 
measures to control inflation and borrowings to promote growth; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what is the action plan of Government to make tax administration 
customer friendly? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S. S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Containment of inflation 
remains high on the agenda of the government, as inflation hurts everybody, 
particularly the poor whose incomes are not indexed to prices. High inflation 
puts pressure on interest rates leading to a rise in project costs and investment. 
It also tends to reduce real interest rates, thereby adversely affecting the savings 
rate. Anti-inflationary policies of the government include strict fiscal and 
monetary discipline, rationalization of excise and import duties of essential 
commodities so that there is no undue burden on the poor, effective supply-
demand management of essential items through liberal tariff and trade 
policies, and strengthening the public distribution system. 
(c) Important steps taken by the Government for making tax 
administration taxpayer friendly are: 
(i) computer assisted services such  as-(a) dissemination of tax related 
information (b) dissemination of tax payer specific information, (c) 
PAN (Permanent Account Number) and TAN  (Tax Account 
Number) related services, (d) e-filing of returns of income, (e) e-
payment of taxes, (0 processing of retruns/refudns, (g) e-filing of TDS 
(Tax Deducted at Source) returns, 
(ii) reducing interface with the tax payers, and 
(iii) opening of help centres for the small tax payers.

Increase in Bank Credit to Agricultural Sector 
150. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: W ill the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have announced to double the Bank credit to 
agricultural sector in the next three years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the financial institutions, including commercial, 
rural and cooperative Banks have failed to reach even half of the farming 
families in India, over the years, if so, details thereof; 
(d) whether still a large number of farmers continue to depend on money-lenders, 
commission agents and other sources to meet their credit needs; and 
(e) what measures Government propose to take to help farmers in meeting their 
credit needs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI S.S. 
PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The targeted increase of 30% in credit 
flow to agricultural in 2004-05 has been exceeded. 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(c) The number of operational holdings in the country is 12.76 crore and over five 
crore Kisan Credit Cards (KCC) have been issued by the Banking system. Apart from 
this there are also a large number of agricultural investment loans being issued by 
Banks which in many cases are out of KCC fold (investment credit is roughly 35% of 
total agricultural loans issued by Commercial Banks). 
(d) and (e) The percentage of indebted families in rural areas on non-institutional 
sources has come down (68.3% in 1971 to 30.6% in 1991). The following measures 
have been taken by the Government to help farmers in meeting their credit needs: 
 
* Banks have been instructed not to insist on collateral or margin for loans upto 
Rs. 50,000/-. 
* Rate of interest on crop loans upto Rs. 50,000/- has been kept at 9% or 
below. 
* Commercial Banks and Regional Rural Banks were advised to make efforts 
to bring into their fold, on average atleast 100 new farmers by each rural 
and semi-urban branch during the year 2004-05. The overall target of 50 
lakh new farmers has been exceeded. 
* Kisan Credit Card has been modified so as to include a component for 
consumption needs. 
* Banks have been advised to advance credit to farmers indebted to money-
lenders.

Natural Gas;

ultra vires; and

include Natural Gas in the Union List? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI

dated 25.3.2004 in Special Reference No. 1/2001 under Article 143(1) of the

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

containing provisions relating to Natural Gas or LNG would be ultra vires to 
that extent.

Misuse of domestic LPG cylinders 
206. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether CNG and LPG are the economical alternative fuel to petrol and 
diesel for use in motor vehicles; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; 
(c) whether any guidelines and approved workstations exist for conversion of 
petrol/diesei vehicles into CNG/LPG vehicles; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) whether it is a fact that most of the private vehicles ply on domestic LPG 
cylinders fitted by local unapproved mechanics, thereby endangering the life and 
property of the passengers and others around; and 
(f) if so, what measures are contemplated to educate and prevent such misuse? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) CNG and LPG have emerged as alternative clean 
fuels to petroi and diesel for use in motor vehicles. Besides the question of 
availability of fuel, the economics of converting petrol/diesei vehicles to 
CNG/LPG vehicles would depend upon the cost of conversion as also the cost of 
fuel, which would vary from place to place. At present, in Delhi, CNG is cheaper 
by about 68% as compared to petrol and 46% as compared to diesel. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. CNG kits are duly approved by the Statutory 
Authorities such as the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI)- 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Pune, the Vehicles Research and Development Establishment (VRDE)-
Ahmednagar; the Indian Institute of Petroleum (IIP)-Dehradun etc. CNG 
cylinders are also approved by the Chief Controller of Explosives, Nagpur. The 
approved CNG kits can be retrofitted on the vehicles by the workshops which 
are duly approved by the Transport Departments of the State Governments. With 
regard to auto LPG, the Central Government have notified the LPG (Regulation 
of Use in Motor Vehicles) Order, 2001 for use of LPG in vehicles. In terms of this 
order, the use of Auto-LPG in motor vehicles is allowed only in case it is 
fitted with a permanent Auto-LPG tank and a conversion kit as approved by the 
authorities/testing agencies as notified in the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 
2001. 
(e) and (f) The following measures have been taken by the Government to 
forestall the misuse of domestic LPG cylinders in vehicles:— 
(i) State Government have been advised to impress upon district 
authorities the need to intensify their supervision of LPG driven 
vehicles and taken action as per law in case of violations. 
(ii) Supplies to domestic LPG distributors are regulated by the Oil 
Marketing Companies(OMCs) in line with the customer population and 
per capita consumption of that market, based on last year's sales for 
the same month. 
(iii) Publicity campaigns are launched by OMCs from time to time to make 
the public aware about the hazards associated with the unauthorized 
use of domestic LPG cylinders as auto LPG.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir.

Statement 
Details of "Looming Water Crisis" highlighted in the Mid Term Appraisal 
Document of Tenth Five Year Plan by Planning Commission 
India is already on the verge of a grave water crisis as brought out below. 
* Per capita availability below 1000 m3 is water scarce. 
* This availability is made up of 200 m3 for domestic/industrial use, 200 
m3 for ecology/maintaining minimum flows and 600 m 3 for food 
security. 
* A minimum per capita storage of 1000 m3 is thus required to meet all the 
three uses. 
* Nine river basins with 20 crore population are already under water scarce 
condition. 
* In India, the per capita availability now is 1820 m3 and per capita storage 
is 207 m3. 
* 631 billion cubic metre (BCM) in Ganga-Brahmaputra is 
unutilisable. Hence actual per capita availability is only 1200 m3. 
* Even if all ongoing and potential storages are completed, per capita storage 
will increase only up to 400 m3. 
194 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* Increasing population will vitiate both per capita availability and per capita 
storage. 
* Improving water use efficiency through proper water management in both irrigated 
and rain fed areas, implementation of watershed programmes and artificial 
recharge of ground water, restoring the traditional water bodies, interlinking of 
rivers, maintaining the water quality standards through pollution abatement 
programmes and downward revision of water supply norms will somewhat 
improve the situation on the water front.

Linking of Rivers 
225. SHRI RK. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether several States are facing heavy floods with the onset of the 
Monsoon this year; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to draw special strategy or 
action plan to get rid of the flood problem in the country; and 
(c) whether solution of the flood problem is possible by linking all the rivers 
of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER-
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) Flood throughout the world cannot be fully controlled. It is to be 
managed to the best of ability on technical merit of the problem from place to 
place. However, Flood Management being within the purview of States, the 
schemes for flood control are planned, funded and executed by the 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
State Governments. The role of Central Government is technical, catalytical and promotional in 
nature. UFA Government gave special emphasis on this issue in the National Common 
Minimum Programme. 
Central Government, however, has also been initiating various measures for assisting the 
States in the management of floods. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog, set up by the Government of 
India in 1976 to look into flood problem and suggest remedial measures, submitted its 
report in 1980. The recommendations of the Rashtriya BarhAyog which formed the 
framework for flood management strategy in the country were formawred to the various State 
Governments for implementation. Several other expert committees were also constituted 
by the Government from time to time to study the problem relating to flood and its 
management, the recommendations of which were also sent to the respective State 
Governments for implementation. Ganga Flood Control Commission for Ganga Basin 
States constituted in 1972 prepared Comprehensive Plans for Flood Management for all the 23 
river systems of Ganga. Likewise, Brahmaputra Board which started functioning at 
Guwahati in 1982 prepared Master Plans for Flood Management for Brahmaputra, Barak 
and its major tributaries. These plans were forwarded to concerned State Governments for 
implementation. 
During 2004, the Government of India had constituted a Task Force for Flood 
Management/Erosion Control under the Chairmanship of Chairman, Central Water 
Commission with representatives of State Governments, various Central Ministries and 
experts as members to examine the problem of flood and erosion in Assam and 
neighbouring States, West Bengal, Bihar and Eastern Uttar Pradesh. The Task 
Force has inter alia recommended taking up of reservior projects as permanent/long 
term measures flood management. 
The Government of India have been taking effective steps in this direction. An agreement was 
reached with Nepal for survey and investigation and preparation of Detailed Project 
Report for Sapta Koshi High Dam Multipurpose Project and Sun Koshi Storage Cum 
Diversion Scheme for which a Joint Project Office has already been opened in Nepal in 
August, 2004. This project has flood control as one of the major benefits. Nepal has also 
agreed for undertaking the joint feasibility study of Kamla and preliminary study of 
Bagmati Multipurpose Project to ascertain likely constratints in implementation of 
these projects so that the same could be appropriately addressed. 
202 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
As regards North-East, the Master Pl ans prepared by Brahmaputra Board 
have emphasized that the flood problem in the Brahmaputra Valley can be solved 
satisfactorily and enduringly only after construction of large storage dams in the 
basin and that too in the upper part of the basin. Keeping this in view, 
investigations of two most promising project namely the Siang Dihang Dam 
Project and the Subansiri Dam Projects were pursued and project reports were 
prepared by the Brahmaputra Board. These projects which are now to be taken 
up in three stages each have since been transferred to National Hydro-electric Power 
Corporation (NHPC) for detailed investigation and implementation. Detailed 
Project Report for another major project namely Tipaimukh Multipurpose Project on 
river Barak has also been prepared which will inter alia have flood control 
benefits in the Barak Valley. The Government of India also approved 
implementation of Pagladiya Multipurpose of Project in Assam, which has flood 
control as a major benefit. In addition to the above, the Government of India has 
also been providing Central assistance to the State Governments to take up 
critical anti erosion/flood management works. 
(c) Based on various studies conducted, National Water Development Agency 
(NWDA) has identified 30 links for preparing Feasibility Reports (FRs). 
NWDA has completed feasibility reports for 14 links under Peninsular Development 
Component and two links under Himalyan Rivers Development Component. The 
storages envisaged in the interlinking of rivers proposals of NWDA under National 
perspective Plan, by virtue of their capacities and diversion of flood water 
through link canals, will inter-alia provide flood modernisation benefits to 
some extent in the respective basins. 
Excess Nitrate in Water 
226. SHRI JANARDHAN POOJARY:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a report by the Central Ground Water Board has revealed nitrate 
concentration in excess of the admissible limit in water in various parts of the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard, State-wise; 
(c) whether consumption of such contaminated water causes cancer or 
damages the nervous system; 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(d) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(e) the action initiated to provide safe water in the affected areas, with 
allocation of funds for the purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Nitrate content in excess of the desirabl e limit of 45 mg/l from ground water 
sources has been reported by Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) in localized 
pockets in various parts of the country. State-wise details of districts parts of 
which are affected by excess nitrate in ground water are given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(c) and (d) As per WHO, the wight of evidence is strongly against a positive 
correlation between nitrate exposures in humans and the risk of cancer. A 
conclusive evidence is yet to be established as regards the relationship 
between nitrite/nitrate and neurological manifestations. 
(e) 'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the reposibility of the 
concerned State Governments to formulate schems to provide people with 
contamination free water. However, CGWB monitors ground water quality 
periodically to map the changes in it and apprises the State Governments of 
the same taking necessary remedial measures. It has also drilled exploratory 
wells tapping contamination free aquifer zones and has handed over these wells 
to the State Governments, free of cost, for utilisation. 
Department of Drinking Water Supply, under the Ministry of Rural 
Development, is also rendering financial and technicial asistance to the States 
for tackling water quality problems in rural areas through a Centrally Sponsored 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). 15% of ARWSP funds 
have been exclusively earmarked for Sub Mission projects for tackling water quality 
problems. With effect from 01.04.1998, powers to sanction Sub Mission 
projects have been delegated to States. Funds amounting to Rs. 1899.64 crores, 
Rs. 1646.29 Crores and Rs.2017.88 Crores were released under ARWSP 
(includign normal ARWSP, Desert Development Programme and Natural 
Calamities) by the Department of Drinking Water Supply during the years 
2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05 respectively.

SHRIMATI AMBIKASONI: SHRI 
SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Governments attention has been drawn to the news-item captioned, 'NCR 
KE SAAT BLOCKON KABHUMIGAT JAL KHATARNAK SATAR PAR', 
appeared in the media; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereon; 
206 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the steps taken to maintain satisfactory level of underground water; 
(d) whether it is a fact that large scale illegal boring activities are taking place 
in the above said districts despite imposing ban on boring activities; and 
(e) whether there is any proposal to identify those new bores and to take 
action against them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Significant decline in ground water levels, in general, has been observed during 
the last decade in certain pockets of the National Capital Region (NCR) 
including South & South-West Delhi, Faridabad, Gurgaon and Ghaziabad 
districts. 
(c) Following steps have been taken to maintain the satisfactory level of ground 
water in the NCR:- 
(i) The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has notified South & 
South-West district of NCT of Delhi, Municipal Corporation of 
Faridabad, Municipal Corporation of Ghaziabad, Gurgaon Town and 
adjoining industrial areas of Haryana for the purpose of regulation of 
ground water development and management. For enforcement of 
regulatory measures in these areas, concerned Deputy 
Commissioners/District Magistrates (DCs/DMs) have been directed under 
Section-5 of Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to take necessary 
action in case of violation of directives of CGWA. 
(ii) The CGWA have issued directions to Group Housing Societies, 
Institutes, Hotels, Industries, Farmnouses etc., in the notified areas of 
Delhi, Faridabad, Gurgaon and Ghaziabad to adopt rain water 
harvesting system. 
(iii) The CGWA is promoting rain Water harvesting and artificial recharge 
through mass awareness and training programmes. 
(iv) Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation, Government of 
India have modified Building Bye-laws (1983) to incorporate 
mandatory provision of roof top rain water harvesting in new 
buildings on plots of 100 sq. mts or more in Delhi through storage of rain 
water runoff to recharge underground aquifer. Similarly, State 
207 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Government of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh Housing Board have made 
rooftop rain water harvesting mandatory in urban areas. 
(v) Technical guidance on rain water harvesting has been provided by the 
Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) to around 2000 agencies including 
Government agencies, educational institutions, private entrepreneurs 
and individuals in the NCR. 
(vi) The CGWB has also implemented 17 projects of rain water 
harvesting for ground water recharge in National Capital City of Delhi. 
These projects have been undertaken in many Government buildings like 
President's Estate, Prime Minister's Office, Shram Shakti Bhawan, 
Sena Bhawan, Vayusenabad etc. Rain water harvesting has also been 
taken up in a big way by CPWD, DDA, NDMC, NGOs, Resident 
Welfare Associations (RWAs), industries and individuals covering 
Government buildings, office complexes, residential buildings & 
colonies, roads & flyovers, hospitals, hotels & institutions, parks, 
farmhouses etc. 
(vii) With a view to encourage rain water harvesting by RWAs/Group 
Housing Societies, the Government of NCT of Delhi is providing 
financial assistance where 50% of the total cost of the project subject 
to a maximum of Rs. 50,000/- is being given as a grant to such 
RWAs/Group Housing Societies, who adopt rain water harvesting. 
(viii) The Government of National Capital City of Delhi has taken many steps 
for setting up of rain water ha rvesting systems. More than 800 
Government buildings have been fitted with rooftop rain water 
harvesting structures. Instructions have been issued by Government 
of NCT of Delhi to all Departments to install rain water harvesting 
structures in existing buildings and make a provision in the estimates 
in respect of new buildings. 
(d) and (e) DCs/DMs of areas notified by CGWA are taking necessary action 
for implementation of directives of the CGWA. As and when a report of illegal 
boring is received, the necessary action is taken by the DC/DM through 
impounding of rig machines, sealing or dismantling of tubewells etc.

Child Education 
*12. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan to take over the responsibility of education to all 
the children of age group six to fourteen years irrespective of the financial capability of 
their parents; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the manner in which hundred per cent education would become possible? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) Provision of Free and Compulsory Education to children of 
6-14 years is a Constitutional mandate. Under the Centrally sponsored scheme of Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan which aims to achieve universal retention at the elementary stage by 
the year 2010, Central Government gives assistance to States, inter alia, for provision of free 
textbooks to all girls and SC/ST boys. Under this scheme, Education Guarantee Scheme 
and Alternative and Innovative Education Centres are also run for children in remote areas 
and those who cannot attend regular schools, and certain other incentives like free uniform 
to girls can also be provided in educationally backward blocks. In addition, Central Assistance 
230 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
is also being given for provision of cooked Mid-Day-Meals to children at the 
Primary stage, and for running residential schools for girls from weaker sections in 
selected educationally backward blocks. Taken together, these measures 
substantially address the problem of participation of children belonging to 
poor families in elementary education.

percentage then that of private independent schools in Delhi and in other parts of 
the country both in class X and XII in 2005 Board examinations. The pass

Government in Delhi and in some other States/UTs are lower both in class X 
and XII as compared to that of private independent schools in 2005 Board

Prohibition of Dowry 
*14. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRI JANARDAN DWIVEDI. 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
232 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the Supreme Court has made a suggestion to Government to make 
such a provision which would make it mandatory for all male Government 
employees to furnish a statement on whether they have accepted dowry and if 
so, the details thereof; 
(b) whether Government would make any such provision for the common people 
also so that the evil practice of dowry may be eradicated; 
(c) if so, by when; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. In the judgement of the Supreme Court dated 
2nd May, 2005 in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 499 of 1997. Union of India and the 
State Governments were directed to consider whether appropriate rules cannot 
be framed for compelling males, seeking government employment, to furnish 
information on whether they had taken dowry and if taken, whether the same has 
been made over to the wife as contemplated by section 6 of the Dowry 
Prohibition Act, 1961 and for calling for such information also from those 
already in employment. 
(b) to (d) No, Sir. The Government does not contemplate making any such 
provision for the common man other than those already included in the Dowry 
Prohibition Act, 1961. As per the Act, giving, demanding or taking of dowry 
are punishable offences. The Dowry Prohibition (Maintenance of Lists of 
Presents to the Bride and Bridegroom) Rules, 1985 have also been notified. 
Metro Rail Services 
*15. SHRI R.P GOENKA: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a proposal has been formulated to make metro 
rail a part of the public transport system for all major cities having a population 
of over 50 lakhs; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including an outline of the plan if any, drawn up, for 
execution over the next ten years, the States which have opted for and the cities 
identified for creating the metro infrastructure and the pattern of funding evolved 
therefor? 
233 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI 
AZAD): (a) and (b) Urban Transport being a State subject, it is for the State 
governments to formulate appropriate proposals for public transport systems in 
their cities. Under the proposed National Urban Transport Policy Government of 
India would encourage all large cities to develop city-specific plans for mass transit 
systems, using such technologies as are appropriate, keeping in view the likely 
demand and other tech no-economic factors. Government would offer financial 
support in the form of equity or viability gap funding, subject to fulfilment of 
specified conditions. 
Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Delhi already have rail based mass transit 
systems. Proposals have been received for expansion of the system in Mumbai and 
Delhi. A proposal has also been received for a rail based mass transit system for 
Bangalore.

2. SHRI RUDRA NARAYAN PANY: Will the Minister of CULTURE be

discovered Buddhist stupas;

structural plans are similar to ones seen at Sarnath, Bihar? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (c) 
Yes, Sir. The Archaeological Survey of India has discovered a large number of 
Buddhist votive stupas from excavations at Udaygiri, Distt. Jajpur, Orissa, 
during the years 2001-2002 and 2002-2003. There are three major groups of votive 
stupas of varying dimensions, made of bricks and stones. These stupas were 
constructed on squarish, rectangular or circular platforms. The bases of some 
stupas have circular depressions for keeping terracotta sealings bearing Buddhist 
incantations. Based on archaeological evidences, these stupas are datable 
variously to circa 1st—-12th century AD. Besides, a votive stupa has been 
discovered at Ratnagiri, District Jajpur, Orissa, during the year 2003-04, 
datable to circa 9th-10th century AD.

Deterioration of Konark Temple 
4. SHRI JANARDAN 
DWIVEDI: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the structure of Konark Temple and its magnificent celestial 
chariot and ..tone sculpture is fast turning into a colossal ruin; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that 25 per cent of its sculptural embellishment etched 
on inert stones, have been defaced by erosion and lost forever; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons for neglecting maintenance of the 
temple; and 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(d) the steps proposed to be taken to preserve the heritage of this temple? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) to (d) The architectural members of the temple built of Khondolite, a soft stone, is 
subject to constant wind action as the temple is located close to the sea. The salt laden 
sea wind causes surface damage to the stone members. This also causes crystallization of 
soluble salts leading to weathering and corrosion of the stone members. 
Following remedial measures are adopted regularly to control weathering of stone 
members and to conserve the heritage. 
(i) Soluble salts are removed by repeated paper pulp treatment. 
(ii) Micro-vegetational and fungicidal growth are being treated chemically. 
(iii) The weathering effects are minimized through stone consolidation. 
(iv) Water tightening and underpinning of the structure are carried out using 
traditional mortar. 
(v) Missing stone members of the adhishtana were restored using the original stone 
members found scattered in the temple complex or with new stones, if 
necessary.

Private National Curriculum Framework, 2005 
16. DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Private National Curriculum Framework, 2005 seeks to draw 
out creativity, eliminate airtight compartmentalization of subject, make education 
more relevant and provide" avenues for greater participation of Panchayati Raj 
institutions and civil society groups in making it a tool for social change; 
(b) if so, whether there is a renewed attempt also to implement three 
language formula, recognizing mother tongue including tribal languages, as best 
medium of instruction; 
(c) if so, whether all these suggestions have been recommended to 
Government; and 
256 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) what are the steps being taken to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) The NCERT has 
been assigned a special role for preparing and promoting a National 
Curriculum Framework (NCF). The National Policy on Education, 1986 
mandates a five yearly review of the various parameters of the Policy. 
Accordingly, consequent on a decision, the process of the review of the NCF 
was initiated by the NCERT through wide ranging consultations and 
deliberations across the country. 
The draft NCF 2005 si nce prepared includes the following salient 
features:— 
(i) It is based on the following four guiding principles:— 
Connecting knowledge of life outside the school, 
Ensuring that learning shifts away from rote methods, 
Enriching the curriculum so that it goes beyond textbooks, 
Making examinations more flexible. 
(ii) The NCF also focuses on the child  as an active learner, thus giving 
primacy to the children's experiences, their voices and their 
participation. It views children as active participants in the 
construction of knowledge, and states that schools should recognize 
the innate ability and creativity of each child to construct his/her own 
knowledge. 
(iii) It recommends the softening of subject boundaries so that children can 
get a taste of integrated knowledge and joy of understanding. 
(iv) It reaffirms faith in panchayati raj institutions to enable people to 
think, decide and act in their coll ective interest, to provide greater 
participation of people in development. 
(b) The NCF 2005 makes a renewed attempt to implement the Three 
Language Formula, emphasizing mother tongue as a medium of instruction 
including tribal languages. 
(c) and (d) The draft NCF 2005 was discussed in the meeting of the 
Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) held on the 7th June, 2005 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
wherein it was decided that the NCF after appropriate modifications, will be 
discussed further and finalized in the next meeting of the CABE to be held in 
August, 2005.

Fear Psychosis due to examination 
33. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the numb er of students suffering from traumatic 
disaster relating to fear of examinations is on the rise; 
281 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the exam-related stress is, sometimes leading 
to suicides; 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take in this regard; 
(d) whether it is a fact that a meeting of experts was held; and 
(e) if so, what are the suggestions/recommendations made by the experts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
The problem of increasing stress among students during examinations and 
instances of some students committing suicide due to failure in examination 
and stress have been engaging the attention of the Government. However, 
there are various contributory factors such as competition, peer & parental 
pressure, fast changing socio and economic conditions, lack of employment 
opportunities and fear of failure in examinations which could become the 
cause of tragedies like suicides among students. 
The Ministry is deeply concerned with the issue of higher stress level among 
students caused by the public examinations at the end of class X and XII 
conducted by various boards, Joint Entrance Examination for NTs and other 
entrance examinations. 
(c) to (e) To address the question of promoting equality in access to 
education as also allow the students to have a stress free environment of joyful 
learning, the Ministry had convened a meeting with Eminent Educationists, 
Principals, representatives from premier Institutions such as the Indian 
Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management, Heads of the 
Boards of Examination and others on 24th March, 2005. It was unanimously 
agreed that there must by systemic reforms to eliminate exam related stress. The 
issue was further discussed in the conference of Council of Boards of Secondary 
Education (COBSE) held on 1st May, 2005, the CBSE has since taken the 
following steps: 
(i) Segregating the syllabus: 
The Board has segregated the syllabus for classes IX & X and also for 
classes XI & XII. The examinations for classes IX & XI based on the 
prescribed syllabus will be conducted by the schools concerned 
282 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
while for classes X & XII, public ex aminations are being conducted by 
the Board. 
(ii) Single theory paper for all subjects: 
The Board has provision for only one theory paper for all subjects in the 
public examinations for classes X & XII. However, other State Boards 
were also requested to have once question paper for each subject in the 
public examinations. 
(iii) Extra time for examination: 
The Board has taken a decision in the recent Governing Body meeting that the 
studetns be allowed an extra 15 minutes time before the commencement 
of the examinations to study the question papers. It is also been decided 
that the question papers will be set in such a way that they can be 
answered in a time period of two and a half hours while the students 
will have a time period of three hours for completion of the question 
paper. 
(iv) Grading pattern: 
The Board has initiated necessary steps for finalizing the pattern of grades 
which would be introduced at the earliest. 
(v) Flexibility in the choice of subjects: 
Presently, the Board offers adequate flexibility in the choice of subjects 
at the senior school level in order to meet the requirements multiple 
intelligence of the students. However, at the secondary level, the Board is 
implementating the National Core Curriculum with a prescribed set of 
subjects. 
(vi)  Provision of differential levels: 
The Board had moved a proposal for provision of differential levels of 
difficulty in the subjects of Mathematics and Sciences at the secondary 
level for students for the secondary level. The matter is under active 
consideration and will be taken up subsequent to the finalization of the 
new curricular framework by NCERT 
(vii) Continuous and comprehensive evaluation: 
The Board conducts public examinations only at the Class X level and 
has given specific instructions to schools to de-stress 
283 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
examinations at the primary and at the middle level by adopting continuous 
and comprehensive evaluation. 
(viii) Internal assessment: 
The Board has taken initiatives to introduce internal assessment in the subjects of 
Mathematics, Sciences and Social Sciences based on project work and assignments. 
This would give adequate thrust on continuous learning in classrooms and 
assessment of the performance of students on a holistic base covering wide range 
of learning skills rather than one short examination at the secondary level.

43. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 35 million children between 6-10 years do not 
attend primary school, while 9 out of 10 of the children do not complete their 
schooling despite a plethora of schemes for education of kids: 
(b) if so, the details of the areas/regions which are hard hit in children 
education; and 
(c) the action plan of the centre to help such regions to complete 
enrolment of all the school-going children? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) As per 
provisional data supplied by the State Governments for the year 2002-03, about 6 
Million children in the age group 6-10 years are not attending school and 
about 63% of the children do not complete class X of the school. State-wise 
Gross Enrolment Ratio (percentage of children enrolled in classes l-V to the total 
population of the age group 6-10) and dropout rates of children in classes I—X 
are given in the Statement (See below) 
(c) Some of the steps taken by the Government to enroll children in 
schools and to reduce dropouts are: 
- Education has been made free for all children between 6-14 years. 
- Providing cooked mid-day-meal to boost the efforts towards 
"Universilisation of Primary Education" by increasing enrolment, 
retention, attendance and simultaneously impacting on the nutrition of 
students in primary classes. 
- Monitoring of attendance by the community. 
- Micro planning and households survey to identify the dropouts and 
reasons therefor. 
- Organising retention drives. 
- Improving the quality of teaching to retain children in school. 
- Organising bridge courses/back to school camps etc. to bring the 
dropouts back into school.

Piracy in film industry 
53. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the film Industry has suffered heavy losses due to 
the prevalent menance of unchecked piracy; and 
317 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(b) the steps taken and being taken to check piracy effectively? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) According to the Federation of Indian Chamber of Commerce 
and Industry (FICCI) the revenue loss from film piracy is about Rs. 1200 Crores annually. 
As far as the Music Industry is concerned, the Indian Music Industry (IMI) has informed 
that the size of the music industry has fallen from Rs. 1000 Crores in 1999 to Rs. 500 
Crores in 2004 due to piracy. The Ministry does not have any other data. 
(b) The Copyright Act, 1957, which fails under the purview of the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development contains, inter alia, legal provisions regarding copyright in 
cinematograph films and music. The responsibility for dealing with offences under the 
Copyright Act rests with the police authorities of the State Governments and Union 
Territory Administrations. Copyright Enforcement cells have been set up in most 
States/UT Administrations headed by a senior police officer to deal with such 
offences. 
Apart from this, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has taken the following 
steps to fight piracy in the film sector: 
• This Ministry has a Plan Scheme to undertake activities relating to anti piracy 
measures. 
• The Ministry has initiated action to formulate appropriate training modules for 
police officers to train them for anti-piracy. 
• In September 2001, Ministry of l&B brought together representatives of the film 
producers, multi-service operators and cable operators who have jointly resolved 
not to exhibit films without valid permission from the copyright holders. 
• Recognizing that high levels of entertainment tax lead to piracy, the Committee for 
Development of the Entertainment Sector, a sub committee of the 24th State 
Information Ministers' Conference, recommended that the rate of entertainment 
tax be lowered to a ceiling of 45%. In the recent SIMCON it was felt that the 
ceiling should be further lowered to 25-30%. 
• The same Committee also recommended appointment of senior police 
318 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
officers in States to work in co-ordination with the entertainment 
industry, as nodal officers. 
• During the Budget of 2003-04, audio CDs were exempted from excise duty to 
do away with the price advantage available to pirated CDs. 
• The Public Service Broadcasting Trust has been entrusted with the task of 
making a film on piracy. 
• The Cable Television Networks Regulation Act has been amended in 2000, to 
prohibit a Cable operator from transmitting or re-transmitting any 
programme or channel for which the Copyright holder has not granted 
him a license. 
• The Ministry has requested Chief Secretaries of all States to advise District 
Magistrates and Superintendents of Police to include anti piracy 
measures in their monthly activity reports. 
• In the meeting of the 25th State Information Ministers, piracy emerged as a 
key concern for most State Governments and some measures were 
considered in order to deter piracy in the film and music industry. 
• This Ministry has also made suggestions for restricting incidence of piracy 
in the film and music sector while considering the on going amendments 
to the Copyright Act. 
• National Film Development Corporation Ltd. has been commissioned to 
make spots for running an anti piracy campaign on prominent national 
and satellite channels. This Ministry has requested industry Associations to 
persuade films stars to work on this campaign in order to make it an 
effective one. 
• This Ministry is consulting FICCI to explore the possibility of enacting an 
Optical Disc Law.
