(b) Recognition of a political party as National Party is governed by the 
provisions of paragraph 6B of the Election Symbols (Reservation and 
Allotment) Order, 1968. Recognition is based on the poll performance of 
political parties at General Election to the House of the People and Legislative 
Assemblies. For recognition as National Party, a political party should satisfy any 
of the following conditions on the basis of general election(s):— 
(i) The candidates set up the party, in any four or more States, at the last 
general election to the House of the People, or to the Legislative Assembly 
of the State concerned, have secured not less than six percent of the total 
valid votes polled in each of those States at that general election; and, in 
addition, it has returned at least four members to the House of the 
People at the aforesaid last general election from any State or States; or 
(ii) At the last general election to the House of the People, the party has 
won at least two percent of the total number of seats in the House of the 
People, any fraction exceeding half being counted as one; and the party's 
candidates have been elected to the House from not less than three 
seats; or 
(iii) The party is recognized as State Party in at least four States. 
330 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Orders regarding grant of recognition are passed as soon as possible after 
compiling the full statistical data regarding the total votes polled and seats won 
by various political parties at the general election(s) concerned. 
(c) As on date, there are 46 political parties, which are recognized as 
State parties in different States. For recognition as State party, a political 
party should satisfy any of the following conditions on the basis of general 
election in the State concerned:— 
(i) At the last general election to the Legislative Assembly of the State, the 
candidates set up by the party have secured not less than six percent of 
the total valid voted polled in the State; and, in addition, the party has 
returned at least two members to the Legislative Assembly of that State 
at such general election; or 
(ii) At the last general election to the House of the People from that State, 
the candidates set up Dy the party have secured not less than six percent of 
the total valid votes polled in the State; and, in addition, the party has 
returned at least one member to the House of the People from that State 
at such general election; or 
(iii) At the last general election to the Legislative Assembly of the State, the 
party has won at least three percent of the total number of seats in the 
Legislative Assembly, (any fraction exceeding half being counted as one), or at 
least three seats in the Assembly, whichever is more; or 
(iv) At the last general election to the House of the People from the State, 
the party has returned at least one member to the House of the People for 
every 25 members or any fraction thereof allotted to that State. 
(d) Registration as political party is governed by the provisions of section 
29Aof the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and the Orders/guidelines 
issued by the Commission from time to time. An association seeking 
registration as political party has to submit an application giving ail the 
particulars/documents required under the said section 29A, and in the 
Registration of Political Parties (Furnishing of Additional Particulars) Order,

82. SHRI C. RAMCHANDRAIAH: 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is proposed to pass a legislation with regard to recognition of 
forest rights for the Scheduled Tribes; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the Bill is likely to be introduced during the current Monsoon 
Session of Parliament; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken so far in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI PR. KYNDIAH): (a) to (d) 
Yes, Sir. The Ministry of Tribal Affa irs has been mandated to formulate a 
comprehensive Central Legislation to redress the historical injustice done to forest 
dwelling Scheduled Tribes by providing for clear assertion of their 
354 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
legal rights on land and other traditional forest rights. This Ministry has 
prepared a draft "The Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005," 
to provide a legislative frame for recognition of the aforementioned rights, in 
consultation with the concerned Ministries, including the Ministry of Law & 
Justice. 
The proposed Bill seeks to recognize such rights on land, minor forest 
produce, etc. for bona fide livelihood needs of the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes. 
The Bill was posted on the website of the Ministry seeking comments of the 
public and all stakeholdes till 10.7.05. The proposed Bill is still a tentative draft 
Bill and to be finalized as per the established procedure taking views and 
comments received from the stakeholders into consideration. No time frame 
can be indicated at this stage.

Water crisis in Delhi 
85. SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that there is an acute shortage of 
drinking water in the capital city Delh i as there is a big gap between demand 
and supply; 
(b) the measures proposed by Government to optimize the capacity to meet 
the shortfall; and 
(c) the short term and long term measures proposed to be taken to address 
the chronic water shortage problem of Delhi? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI 
AZAD): (a) to (c) The Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has informed that against the total 
requirement of 850 million gallons per day (mgd) of water in Delhi, it is 
supplying, on an average, 675 mgd of water in Delhi for a population of about 
140 lakhs. This works out to about 210 Itrs. per capita per day. 
With a view to further increase the availability of drinking water, the DJB has 
constructed water treatment plants at Sonia Vihar and Nangloi with a total 
capacity of 180 mgd. In addition water treatment plants at Dwarka, Bavana and 
Okhla with a total capacity of 80 mgd have also been planned, DJB has also taken 
action to reduce the seepage losses and recycling of waste water at existing water 
treatment plants with a view to further add to the availability of water in Delhi.

National Slum Development Programme 
t97. SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV. Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that no target has been fixed under the National Slum 
Development Programme; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the details of the data on the basis of which problem of slums is solved; and 
(d) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) and 
(b) As per the provisions of National Slum Development Programme (NSDP), the 
implementation of the programme is with the State Governments. Hence, the State 
Governments formulate specific plans, programmes and schemes for development of 
slums in various towns/ cities as per their priorities and made necessary provisions 
therefor, in their respective State plans. 
(c) Since the inception of NSDP, each year the Planning Commission allocates the 
State-wise funds on the pro-rata basis of slum population of States/UTs, keeping a 
minimum amount reserved for smaller States. 
(d) With a view to ameliorate the living conditions of slum dwellers a programme 
known as National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) was launched at national 
level by the Government in 1996 for the development of urban slums. 
Beside, a centrally sopnsored schemes called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana 
(VAMBAY) was launched on 2.12.2001 with a view to ameliorate the conditions of the 
urban slum dwellers living below the poverty line who do not possess adequate shelter. The 
Scheme has the primary objective to facilitate adequate construction and upgradation of 
the dwelling units for the slum dwellers and to provide health and enabiling urban environment 
through community toilets under Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, a component of the Scheme.

major bio-technology power, but if we are unable to predict in a reliable and 
robust manner such a basic thing like the Indian Monsoon which is so central 
to the existence of India even today, I am afraid, Sir, much of our scientific 
and technological expertise would not have much meaning to the large 
sections of our population. So, my second request to the Minister would be to 
have a look at what the scientific assessment of the monsoon model is really 
today. There is a consensus that it has not served us. If it has not served us 
well, where do we go from here? Is it still going to be a gamble; is it still 
going to be fire-fighting next year — fire-fighting for floods and fire-fighting 
for droughts in some other regions? 
Sir, my third point which I would like to raise relates to the 
recommendations of the Twelfth Finance Commission and go directly to the 
short term issue of flood and drought that the States are facing. Gujarat, 
Madhya Pradesh, Himachal and Uttaranc hal have faced severe problems of 
floods. Mr. Vikram Verma raised the question of flood relief for Madhya 
Pradesh. The speakers from Gujarat raised the question of flood relief for 
Gujarat. Sir, what I would like to ask the hon. Minister is this. That the Report 
of the Twelfth Finance Commission which was submitted some months back, 
during the Budget Session, made a large number of far-reaching 
recommendations concerning calamity relief. It made recommendations 
relating to the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF); and it made recommendations 
relating to the NCCF, the National Calamity Contingency Fund. It made 
recommendations both on the financing of these mechanisms, and more 
importantly, in the working of these mechanisms to make it much more 
effective. Now, for example, Sir, just to  take a point that my senior colleague 
Mr. Vayalar Ravi had made and just to buttress the point that he made, in para 
9.12, the Twelfth Finance Commission says, "We find considerable 
justification in widening the list of calamities which may be covered by our 
recommendations". The definition of natu ral calamity as applicable at present 
may be extended to cover landslides, av alanches, cloudburst and pest attacks. 
Avalanches, we know, Sir, was a very natural calamity that overtook the State 
of Jammu and Kashmir some months ago. And so on and so forth. Sir, the 
point I want to make is that a large number of operational recommendations 
which were made by the Twelfth Finance Commission relating to the size of 
the Calamity Relief Fund, relating 
426 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to the size of the National Calamity Contingency Fund, and the manner in 
which these two funds would be operated, I would like the hon. Minister to 
enlighten us on whether these recomme ndations have been accepted by the 
Government, and whether these improvem ents that have been suggested by 
the Twelfth Finance Commission have actually been put into practice. 
Finally, Sir, I would say that every time we have a discussion on 
floods and drought, the issue of inter-lin king of rivers is raised. And I would 
like to reiterate that this is an issue that is fraught with grave political, 
ecological and social consequences and we should hasten slowly in the matter 
in spite of the enthusiasm that has been shown by many people, by many 
scientists, by many distinguished technocrats whom I will not name--they 
have expressed support for the scheme--but I do believe that the weight of 
technological, economic and ecological opinion is that we should hasten 
slowly. There may well be place for inte r-linking of specific rivers like the 
Ken and the Betwa, as put out by the Ministry of Water Resources but to 
imagine that we are going to be able to solve our annual problems of floods 
and drought by a massive programme of inter-linking of rivers, in my view, 
Sir, there would be no greater calamity than massive inter-linking of rivers. 
Thank you. 
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Thank you very 
much, Mr. Vice-Chairman. Some time back, in reply to a supplementary on a 
Starred Question, the Minister for Science and Technology had made a 
statement in this House that the present system does not permit us to make 
week-by-week and district-by-district prediction of the rainfall. I had 
proposed a Short Duration Discussion on that matter, and since it has not 
turned up, I am going to take advantage of today's discussion on the drought 
and flood situation to raise some of the points I raised there, particularly 
because Mr. Jairam Ramesh happened to  have raised some of these points 
now. 
The discussion is taking place towards the end of July and, therefore, 
we are discussing flood and drought. If the discussion had happened towards 
the mid-June this year, then we would have probably discussed only drought. 
Because it was at that time, that th e Prime Minister had called even an 
emergency meeting in order to exam ine how to face drought and famine 
situation in the country. Later on, the rains came; all the same, whereas the 
Indian Meteorological Department had predicted an excess of 19 per cent in 
the month of June, the estimate was re vised to (-)34 per cent by the same 
institute in Bangalore. Consequently, the estimates of the crop 
427 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
were generally scaled down, and after the rain situation improved, recently 
the Minister for Food and Agriculture made a statement that the situation was 
satisfactory and the situation of agricultural commodities would be very good. 
But what requires to be discussed is  not so much the disaster caused by 
the floods, or the sufferings caused by the drought. What is important is, 
whereas for the country as a whole th e rainfall is generally satisfactory, 
particularly if you take into account th e availability of water in countries like 
Israel, why is it that we are facing the problem of coexistence of floods and 
drought in the same country? Coexistence both in the time dimension and in 
the space dimension. As of today, in some States, so many people have said, 
there are floods, in others there is drought. In the month of June we were 
facing an acute situation, a threat of famine and now we are facing a situation 
which is quite different. 
I had proposed that the disasters should not be used as an instrument 
for refurbishing State-finances. R.K. Laxman's famous cartoon shows, in a 
particular area "famine relief fund" banner being replaced by "Flood relief 
fund." Either way, I think, there is a matter of encroachment on river beds 
which results in flood disasters and there are some regions which are 
perennially drought-affected. 
The important thing in today's epoch of knowledge is, do we have 
knowledge of that and if we have knowledge, I think, adequate measures can 
be taken by both the farmers and other people who have stakes in regular 
rainfall to protect themselves. As the Minister for Science and Technology 
himself stated, 'we do not have any system of prediction which can give 
week-by-week and district-by-district forecast of rain.' If that is the situation, I 
would say, a big question arises about justification of continuation of the 
Meteorological Department itself as far as agriculture is concerned because 
farmers are not interested in the annual averages or in the national averages. 
The crops depend upon actual day-to-day, week-to-week rainfall. If the 
rainfall is not there, he wants the rainfall and once the rains start coming, he 
wants the rains to stop. That is the situation in agriculture. As far as 
agriculture is concerned the question is: Is there sufficient degree of 
confidence that can be put in the meteorological prediction? It is 
understandable that we do not have that system. I have seen in many countries 
like Australia, for example, on the radi o they are giving week-by-week and 
even tehsil-by-tehsil prediction, or that kind of a block.   Not only prediction, 
the radio also gives advice to the farmers on the

necessary steps that they have to take. Similarly, when we are flying in by air, 
we are told what kind of weather to ex pect at the destination. If that is 
possible, then, I have a feeling that the meteorological department does not 
have the kind of personnel that is necessary for making prediction that are 
relevant to agriculture who have some kind of a personal knowledge of 
agriculture.

Coordination in Poverty Alleviation Schemes 
*46. SHRI NAND KISHORE Y ADAV: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that for alleviating poverty in rural areas of the 
country it is necessary to remove unemployment; 
(b) if so, whether is is also a fact that many schemes are being run by 
Government at present for providing employment opportunities; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that people are not getting desired benefits of 
these schemes in the absence of mutual coordination among all the schemes; 
and 
(d) if so, the details of corrective steps Government propose to take for proper 
implementation of the said scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (DR. RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (d) Removal of unemployment is one of the necessary 
measures for the alleviation of poverty in the rural areas of the country. 
The Ministry of Rural Development is implementing two major 
employment generation Schemes namely Swarnyajanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana 
(SGSY) and Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) to provide self and 
wage employment to the families living below the poverty line in the rural areas of 
the country. The Government have also launched a new wage employment 
Scheme namely National Food For Works Programme (NFFWP) in 150 most 
backward districts of 27 States of the country to generate supplementary wage 
employment and providing food security through creation of need based 
economic, social and community assets in these districts.  The NFFWP will 
be open to the rural poor who are in need of wage employment-arid desire to do 
manual unskilled work. This programme will be replaced by the National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, the Bill for which has been introduced 
in the Parliament. 
In order to implement the schemes properly, the Ministry of Rural 
Development places special emphasis on monitoring and evaluation of its 
programmes being implemented through review by Union Ministers with Chief 
Ministers and other State Ministers concerned with the programmes of the 
Ministry, Performance Review Committee, Area Officer's Scheme,

*47.      SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:

(a) whether India and the United Stat es signed a MoU for training and

of America (USA) was signed on April 13, 2005.

*58.      SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRIR.K.ANAND: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have ascertained the facts regarding reported export of 
adulterated chillies, if so, the details thereof; 
(b) whether Government have taken up the issue on behalf of Indian exporters, if 
so, what steps are taken, if not, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether WTO agreements provide for sanitary-standards, if so, are they 
standardised, if so, the details thereof, if not. the reasons therefor; and 
(d) whether Government have also ascertained that the 
sanitary-standards are not used as non-tariff barriers against agro-exports 
from developing countries, if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The reports regarding export of adulterated chillies refer 
mostly to the presence of the prohibited Sudan I to IV dyes in chilli exported to 
European Union (EU). Since 2003, European Commission has issued about 61 
rapid alerts claiming presence of Sudan dyes in chillies/chilli products exported 
from India or in food products exported from India or in food products manufactured 
in the EU using chilli powder/chilli products in sourced from India. However, in 
February-March, 2005, Food Standard Agency (FSA), United Kingdom, 
ordered recall of food stuffs contaminated with Sudan dyes. The chilli powder 
claimed to have been used in the manufacture of recalled products in UK was 
exported in 2002, before the introduction 
40 

[27 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
of the mandatory testing regime of the Spices Board for chilli powder/ chilli 
products. 
Government has expressed its concern to the EU authorities over the manner and the 
procedure governing the issuance of rapid alerts. 
(c) The Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreement of WTO provides for 
notification of sanitary standards prior to their enforcement in order to provide trading 
partners an opportunity to comment thereon and these comments have to be taken into 
account before finalizing and enforcing the standards/measures. 
(d) Sanitary and phytosanitary standards are not to be used as non-iariff barriers. 
Under the SPS agreement, WTO member countries are permitted to impose only 
those requirements/measures, which are based on scientific principles and are needed to 
protect public health. The Government can challenge another country's food safety or 
plant health requirements can challenge another country's food safety or plant health 
requirements on the ground that they are not justified by scientific evidence. The 
transparency in the SPS measures discourages countries to use them as non-tariff 
barriers.

229. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will th e Minister of COMMERCE AND

Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA) has been signed between India and 
Singapore by Prime Ministers of the two countries on 29th June, 2005 in New 
Delhi.

Sanitary and phytosanitary standards for agro and farm products 
243. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRIR.K.ANAND:  
        SHRI KB. KRISHNAMURTHY:  
         SHRI HARISH RAWAT: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the WTO agreement provide for Sanitary and Phytosanitary 
standards for agro and farm products; 
(b) if so, what is the mechanism to prescribe such standards; 
(c) what are the guarantees to avoid such standards from being used as non-
tariff barriers; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to enhance Sanitary and Phytosanitary 
Standards of the country's exports? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. The Agreement on 
the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary measures provides for Sanitary 
and Phytosanitary standards for agro and farm products. 
(b) The mechanism for providing such standard is through notifying the new 
or any amendment in the existing stan dards to the WTO, in case, these 
standards are different from the international standards as set by the 
International Plant Protection Convention (IPCC) or such standards would 
have significant trade effect. 
(c) The SPS Agreement in WTO provides that the Sanitary and 
Phytosanitary standards are not to be used as non-tariff barriers. In case, the 
exporter feels that any WTO Member is  using these as non-tariff barrier, the 
Government has the right to ask for the scientific evidences which led to 
imposition of such Sanitary and Phytosanitay measures. The SPS agreement 
has been provided with clear and detailed rights and obligations for food safety and 
plant health measures which affect trad e. Countries are permitted to impose 
only those requirements which are needed to protect health, and these 
requirements have to be based on scientific principle. The Government can 
challenge another country's food safety or plant health requirements on the 
ground that they are not justified by 
58 

[27 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
scientific evidence. The procedures and decisions used by the country in 
assessing the risks to food safety or plant and animal health has to be made 
available to other countries on request. This brings in the transparency in the SPS 
Measures which discourages countries to use SPS measures as non-tariff 
barriers. 
(d) In order to enhance sanitary and phytosanitary standards of the 
country's exports, following major steps have been taken: 
(i) Certification agencies have been established; 
(ii) Export Inspection Councils have been strengthened; 
(iii) Capacity building exercise of the exporters through trainings, 
seminars, etc. have been undertaken; 
(iv) Duty free import of equipments such as panels etc. for meeting the SPS 
Standards have been allowed; 
(v) Residue monitoring plans for specified commodities are being carried out; 
(vi) compulsory testing regimes have been put in place for certain 
specified commodities before consignment are exported out; and 
(vii) exporters are being given financial assistance for quality testing of certain 
specified exportable produces.

Sanitation facilities in rural India 
311. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR:  Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number and percentage of population in rural India, particularly the 
Northern States who have still no access to sanitation facilities even 58 years 
after Independence; and 
(b) the progress made In providing such facilities during the Ninth and Tenth 
Five Year Plans so far; and the expenditure incurred thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) As per Census 2001,10.80 
crore rural households representing 78.11% of total number of rural 
households in the country, did not have access to sanitation facilities. The 
information related to Northern States is given in the enclosed Statement (See 
below). 
(b) To accelerate pace of rural sanitati on coverage in India, a centrally 
sponsored programme, namely Central Rural Sanitation Programme (CRSP), was 
introduced in 1986, and restructured as Total Sanitation Campaign in the year 
1999.51.12 lakh household toilets were constructed under CRSP during the Ninth 
Plan with total expenditure of Rs. 892.76 crore. Under TSC, 1.43 crore household 
toilets have been constructed during the Ninth and Tenth Plans so far. In addition, 
under the TSC, 1.5 lakhs school toilets, 0.25 lakhs Anganwadi toilets and 4,933 
community complexes were also constructed during this period. Rs 1221.47 crore 
has been spent on sanitation promotion under TSC during the Ninth and Tenth 
Plans.

Development of KBK districts of Orissa 
312. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the total amount allocated till 31 st March, 2005 under the long-term action 
plan formulated and implemented for all round development of Kalahandi, 
Boiangir and Koraput (KBK) districts of Orissa; 
(b) the economic, educational and social upliftment in overall living 
standard of residents of the said districts due to allocation of the said amount; 
(c) whether it is a fact that there has not been any expected improvement in the 
overall living standard of natives of the said districts in comparison to the 
amount allocated by Government; and 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor and the action being taken by Government for 
improving their living standards? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) Total amount of 
Rs. 4287.65 crores, including Additional Central Assistance/Special Central 
Assistance of Rs. 943.95 crore, flowed to the KBK districts from 1998-99 to 
2004-05. 
. (b) The following major achievements have been made in different sectors of the 
KBK districts to raise the economic, educational, social and overall living 
standards of the people of the KBK region. 
* 2 lakh old, infirm and indigent persons are being covered annually under 
Emergency Feeding Programme. 
* 9.42 lakh children under the age group 0-6 and other beneficiaries have 
been covered under Special Nutrition Programme annually. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2005] 
* 90 Mobile Health units are functioning in 80 blocks of the KBK 
districts providing treatment to nearly 13 lakh patients annually at their 
doorsteps. 
* Out of 1324 watersheds, 314 watersheds are taken up under the 
programme. 39,520 ha. of area has been treated so far. 
* Afforestation over an area of 1.25 lakh ha. has been made through 644 
VSS and 144.13 lakh mandays have been generated. 
* 400 forty seated residential hostels for girls have been constructed and 
operationalised. All the hostels have been provided with basic 
amenities. Prematric scholarships have been provded to 16,000 girl 
students annually. 
* To enhance access to growth and service centres, 266 roads have been 
improved, 407 culverts and 44 bridges have been constructed. 
* 13,151 tube wells/sanitary wells have been installed to provide safe 
drinking water to the rural poor. 
* 645 LIPs and 26MIPs have been constructed. As a result, additional 
irrigation potential of 16,480 ha. have been created. 
As a result of the aforesaid achievements, the follwoing impacts have been 
visualized in different spheres. 
* Enrolment rate in primary schools in KBK districts has gone up to 
110.36 in.2004-05 from 75.89 in 1996-97. Similarly, the enrolment rate 
in upper-primary schools in KBK districts has gone up to 65.32 in 
2004-05 from 56.39 in 1996-97. 
* Dropout rate in primary schools in KBK districts has been reduced to 
28.93 in 2004-05 from 57.13 in 1996-97. Similarly, the dropout rate in 
upper-primary schools in KBK districts has been reduced to 43.73 in 
2004-05 from 79.10 in 1996-97. 
* Female literacy rate has increased to 29.10 in 2001 from 15.87 in 1991. 
At the same time the overall literacy rate has increased to 43.30 in 2001 
from 29.24 in 1991. 
* Irrigation potential has increased to 33.71% in 2002-03 from 28.56% in 
1998-99. 
* Milk collection per day has increased to 12,930 Itr. in 2003-04 from 
7,814 Itr. in1998-99. 
126 

[27 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA

(d) Does notarise. However, the Government are keen and have been

(d) Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to 
promote India's textile exports in the international markets. Some of the 
important initiatives taken are: 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1.4.1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(ii) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has 
launched Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). The Mission 
comprises four mini-missions, which are being jointly implemented by 
the Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of Textiles. One of the 
important ingredients of the Mission is to improve cotton processing 
facilities by upgrading/modernizing in existing ginning and pressing 
facilities and setting up of new market yards/improvement of 
existing market yards.

scheme titled "Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme" 
(TCIDS) has been launched.

and maximum value addition within the country. Except for 
mandatory excise duty on man-made filament yarns and man-made 
staple fibres, the whole value addition chain has been given excise 
exemption option.

been allowed at concessional rate  of customs duty to encourage 
investments and to make our textile products competetive in the 
global market. The cost of machinery has also been reduced through 
fiscal policy measures.

Decline in textile exports 
† 333. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) the decline in the export of textiles from India and percentage increase in the export of 
textiles from China after the end of 'quota raj' since January 2005; 
(b) the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to ensure that textile export industry could 
sustain itself in the competitive market and by when results thereof are likely to be 
achieved? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) 
According to the provisions DGCI&S data for January-March 2005, the exports of 
textiles and clothing (including handicrafts, jute and coir) had  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [27 JULY, 2005] 
amounted to Rs. 14,857 crores during the period January-March, 2005 as compared to 
the exports of Rs. 19,178 crores during the corresponding period of 2004, showing a 
decline of 22.5%. However, as per the latest available DGCI&S provisional data, 
there has been a positive growth of 13.7% in textile exports during the month of Apirl, 
2005 compared to April, 2004. 
European Union (EU) and United States (US) account for more than 60% of 
India's textile exports. The trade data of EU/US authorities show increased textile 
imports from India and China in the post quota period. According to the US Trade Data, 
the US textiles and clothing imports from China have increased by 60.02% and from 
India by 29.49% during the period January-May, 2005 in comparison to the 
corresponding period of previous year. According to EU Trade Data, China has recorded 
a growth of 46.3% and India 12.2% in the EU-15 imports of textiles and clothing 
Kerns, during the period January-March, 2005 in comparison to the corresponding 
period of previous year; 
(b) The main reasons attributed to the decline in textile exports during January-
March '05 are as follows: 
(i) There has been a downward pressure on prices, consequent upon dismantling of 
quota regime. 
(J) China has been able to withstand the downward pressure on prices as it has large 
production capacities with economies of scale. 
(Hi) The reduction in DEPB rates in September, 2004 had the effect of squeezing 
margins of Indian exporters. The fall in exports has been more pronounced 
in cotton textiles where the cut in DEPB rates were the deepest. 
(C) Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to strengthen 
Indian textile industry for meeting the growing global competition. Some of the important 
initiatives taken are: • 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made operational 
from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and upgradation of the 
sector. 
(I) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has launched 
Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). The mission 
162 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
comprises four mini-missions, which are being jointly implemented by the 
Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of Textiles. One of the important 
ingredients of the Mission is to improve cotton processing facilities by 
upgrading/modernizing the existing ginning and pressing facilities and setting 
up of new market yards/improvement of existing market yards. 
(iii) The Government has launched a Centrally Sponsored Scheme titled 
"Apparel Park for Export Scheme" for imparting focused thrust for setting up 
of apparel manufacturing units of international standards at potential growth 
centres to give fillip to exports. 
(IV) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, a scheme titled 
Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme" (TCIDS) has been 
launched. 
(v) The fiscal duty structure has been generally rationalised to achieve growth and 
maximum value addition within the country. Except for mandatory excise 
duty on man-made filament yams and man-made staple fibres, the whole value 
addition chain has been given excise exemption option. 
(vi) The imports of specified textiles and garment machinery items has been 
allowed at concessional rate of customs duty to encourage investments 
and to make our textile products competitive in the global market. The cost 
of machinery has also been reduced through fiscal policy measures. 
(vii) Duty-free imports of 21 items of trimmings and embellishment items are 
allowed to the garment exporters, upto 3% of their actual export performance 
during the previous year. 
(viii) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its seven branches and apparel 
Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various courses/programmes to 
meet skilled manpower requirements of textile industry especially apparel 
in the field of design, merchandising and marketing. 
(ix) Facilities by way of eco-testing laboratories have been created to enable 
exporters to get the garments/textiles pre-tested for conforming to the 
requirements of importing countries. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 JULY, 2005] 
(x) 100% Foreign Direct Investment is allowed in the textile sector under 
the automatic route. 
(xi) The Government has de-reserved the readymade garments, hosiery and 
knitwear from the SSI sector. 
The above initiatives have helped the textile export industry in sustaining itself in 
the global market.

Re: Grave situation prevailing in Gurgaon due to agitation by workers 
of Honda motor cycles and scooters India 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir. with your 
permission I would like to draw the attention of the House to the very, very grave 
situation which has come to prevail in Gurgaon, Haryana, as a result of the agitation 
by the workers, and the attitude of the management of the Honda Company. I 
think it is necessary to put the whole issue in proper perspective. I visited the 
place, and, particularly, the General Hospital, 
168 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Gurgaon, yesterday along with the Member - elect of this House, Mrs. 
Brinda Karat. 
Sir, the situation prevailing there is very, very unfortunate. After what 
happened day-before-yesterday, which all of us have seen over the television; 
the electronic media, the situation c ontinued to remain very critical in 
Gurgaon yesterday as well. In fact, in front of our eyes, there was a second 
round of lathicharge and firing of teargas shells within the hospital premises 
itself. 
Now, sir, I will come to the issue which sparked off a sequence of this 
very unfortunate development. It arises out of the flagrant violation of labour 
laws enacted by this august House along with the other august House. 
There are several provisions in our laws about trade unions rights, and as 
per international covenant of the ILO also, those laws have to be respected 
in the country because certain questions are also coming up now in the 
context of what happened day-before-yesterday, and yesterday that whether 
this will, actually, have a negative e ffect or an adverse effect on the 
investment climate of the country. I think we have to understand that 
whosoever is, actually, investing and running a facility in this country will 
have to abide by the laws of this country as much as they abide by the 
laws of their home countries wherever they continue to carry on economic 
activities. 
Now, Sir, a lot of things are being said, but this entire chain of events 
started in December last,—the present Government in Haryana had not 
come in place—from the earlier Government itself, in December 2004, 
when one of the Managers of the Honda Company blatantly kicked a 
worker. If you look at the situation in the Honda Company, there are about 
1600 workers who are on the permanent roles and 1400 are temporary 
workers, and there are stiff conditions for the conferment of the jobs of 
these workers. In spite of the persistent efforts of the workers to register a 
trade union, that could not take place earlier. Now , these things have 
been happening, and there is a grave at mosphere of uncertainty there 
among the workers, and it led to the protest demonstration day-before-
yesterday and led to an altercation with the police. Now, I know—the hon. 
Home Minister is sitting here—that for the Government of India to intervene 
directly, that is not possible. But, I think it is possible for the Government 
of India to send advisories to the State Government. Sir, the situation that 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [27 JULY, 2005] 
is prevailing there is actually an expression of a total collapse of the credibility 
of the local Administration. In fact, yesterday's incident— if you look at— took 
place, was triggered off by the presence of the Deputy Commissioner there 
who is widely believed to have spearheaded the barbaric attack on the 
workers day-before-yesterday, and the Superintendent of Police, 
Gurgaon also played a very, very destructive role in handling the situation day-
before-yesterday. Sir, we are aware of the Government's decision to have a 
judicial inquiry ordered in this case. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Everything will be covered under the judicial inquiry.

Chairman, Sir, to begin with, I would like to complement the Ministry of Home 
Affairs, which means the Home Minister. I would like to compliment the Ministry of 
Home Affairs of the previous Government also because this is an on-going 
struggle, an on-going combat and every Home Ministry and every Government 
has been doing its best. We are fortunate to have, notwithstanding the 
incidents we see on the television, extremely competent agencies both in our 
police, in our internal security organisations and in our intelligence. The subject of 
today's discussion is cross border terrorism 
226 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and terrorist acts. I do not know whether the choice of word has been by design 
or by accident, but these are indeed two separate things. Cross border 
terrorism means people who come across the border, and terrorist acts mean 
people who are already in situ. I think the attack on Ayodhya is a good example 
of what is the subject of this discussion. So far as the attack on Ayodhya is 
concerned, the preparation for the attack started off in Mendhar in Jammu and 
Kashmir. Arms were brought across put in a specially constructed Tata Sumo 
brought all the way from Mendhar to Panipat. The people who carried out the 
attack came from Nepal. They stayed in a safe house; married up with the 
arms and ammunition and then they carried out this attack. That means, 
people came from across the border and there were people inside the border 
who could support them. The fight is against the both. What is this situation? 
Cross border terrorism is coming from the west, that is, the border with 
Pakistan. The Pakistan border, regardless of what we may say, is 
reasonably well defended. We have got a fence. Everything is in position. I 
think the terrorists from Pakistan who are coming across, notwithstanding the 
incident of Ayodhya, are finding it more and more difficult to get across. Of course, 
the fencing along the LoC has been damaged due to the recent snowfall. I 
hope it will be made ready in time. But our gaps are in the east and on the 
Nepal border. The eastern border is wide open. The Border Security Force, 
as all of you know, is meant to defend or watch a distance of about 30 to 40 
kilometers which is the distance they watch in the western sector. In the 
eastern sector in West Bengal, Tripura and Assam a single BSF Battalion is 
covering nearly 70 to 90 kilometers. In Tripura, they are covering 90 
kilometres. I think, there were decision taken that they will move the BSF fact 
to the eastern sector, but that has not taken place yet. Sir, I would, through you, 
urge the Government and the Minister to give a thought to the eastern sector 
because the eastern sector is a backdoor which is more or less wide 
open. 
The second is the border with Nepal. It is supposed to be an unfenced 
border which is not manned because of the special relationship we have with 
Nepal. But now we have felt the necessity to keep a border guarding force on 
the Nepal border also. We have given it to the SSB. Now with due respect to the 
Government and to the Force, this is not a very high grade Force as yet. If you 
insist on making the SSB guard the border, please see to it that the SSB 
comes up to the standards of the BSF as soon as 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [27 JULY, 2005] 
possible because this is a wide open border through which all these 
incidents are taking place. 
Really speaking, there are three types of terrorisms in India, that is, Jehadi 
terrorism, Naxalite terrorism and North Eastern terrorism based on ethnic groups. 
To my mind, the biggest threat that is confronting India today is the Naxalite 
terrorism which is holding the entire centre of India, In this, the biggest weapon is 
good governance and police reform. This is the most dangerous form of terrorism 
which is threatening our country and I do think that the Centre's decision that the 
States will combat Naxalite terrorism on their own is a mistaken decision so 
far. I do think that there has to be a coordinated activity between the States. In 
the North East, in Jammu and Kashmir, the lead agency de factor became the 
Army. That is spread across the inter-State borders. So operations could be 
continuously carried out. But when you are using a police force to contain a 
particular type of terrorism and you say that it has to be by the States, I think this 
is not the right method of tackling the Naxalite terrorism. There has to be a 
certain methodology worked out in the North East. There was a lot of talk that the 
North Eastern Council should be made responsible at one point of time. But it did 
not work due to various reasons. The Centre has got to explore ways and 
means whereby the Naxalite-infested States, namely, the seven in number, 
could form some sort of a common grid. The Centre must impress upon the 
States to create a similar organisation that is there in the North-East and in 
Jammu and Kashmir, that is, a unified headquarter. Here, of course, there 
will be various elements in it. But, until these States seriously set up 
organisations like unified headquarters, it will not work. It has been 
mentioned, time and again, that good governance is the key to tackling the 
Naxalite activity. All the areas where the Naxalite activities take place are the 
tribal areas. They are the most under-developed areas in underdeveloped States. 
Now, how do we go about it? We have a federal structure whereby everything 
has to go through the States and, I think, the Prime Minister himself is worried 
about it because the vast amount of resources are going into good 
governance, but the delivery system at the grassroots level remains the 
same. So, my suggestion, as always been, is please create Special 
Development Zones. And, whether the system of governance will be through the 
States, through the Centre, or the amalgamation of both, these have to be 
worked out, because unless you get good governance, you will not be able to fight 
the 
228 

[27 JULY, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Naxalite menace. 
As far as police reforms are concerned, it is, of course easy to say that one 
must tackle the root-cause of Naxafism or, any other form of terrorism, for that 
matter. But the projection of the Government in most of these cases is the 
police force, and the police force has to be reformed not only at the top level, 
but.critically, it must be reformed at the lowest level, that is at the level of the 
Thana. Today, your police, force is discredited because it is not functioning at the 
level where it comes in contact with the people, and that is, not at the level of the 
States headquarters, but it is at the level of the Thana. Unless you get good, well-
trained police force, well-equipped, well-motivated one, working at the Thana 
level, I am afraid that this is not going to work. A mention was made that 
warnings are conveyed to States. I would just like to say that it is very difficult to 
convey warnings with any specifics. It cannot say that there will be an attack on 
Ayodhya on such and such date and at such and such time; it has to be a 
general term. And, under those warnings, every religious institution and, 
particularly, the temples, are under threat in this country at any time. 
In conclusion, let me say that our people are eminently sensisble. In spite 
of the various problems that we have got, the aim of these attacks on temples are 
obviously to weaken the communal harmony. But I think, our people have got 
enough common sense, enough goodwill. So, in spite of what we say, from 
time to time, notwithstanding instances which have taken place earlier, I don't 
think we are going to see any major communal outbreak in this country 
because, as you say, whether in Jammu and Kashmir or in the North-East, 
people of India also want peace. Thank you.

†*62 PROF R.B.S. VARMA: 
SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL:†† 
Will the Minister of OCEAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a team of Indian Scientists is being sent by 
Government to Antarctica for research works: 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the subject on which the Indian Scie ntists would undertake research at 
Antarctica; and 
(d) by when the task would be completed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A scientific 
expedition team to Antarctica is being sent annually since 1981 by the 
Government of India. So far 24 such  expeditions have been successfully 
launched. Each year the expedition is being launched in the month of 
December/January in a chartered ve ssel. The expedition team has two 
components viz; summer and winter. The summer team will carry out the 
scientific activities and will come back in the month of March next year 
leaving behind the winter team. However the winter team will stay back in 
the Indian Antarctic Station 'Maitri' for carrying out various scientific 
experiments and will come back to the main land when the next expedition

technical personnel belonging to various scientific institutes/universities and 
13 logistic personnel drawn from Indian Army are participating.

fields Meteorology & Atmospheric Sc ience; Earth Science & Glaciology;

asked a very important question. I wish to mention that global warming is a 
real issue that the world community is confronted with and one of the things

from the Government of Orissa, the debt burden of the Government of Orissa, 
as on 31st March, 2005, is Rs. 34190.75 crores.

undertaken by the Government of Orissa from 2000-01 to 2004-05 as per the 
MoU signed with Government of India, by 2004-05 (RE), Government of 
Orissa has been able to reduce the revenue deficit as a percentage of revenue 
receipts by 24.59 percentage points from 43.74% to 19.15%. The fiscal 
deficit of the State has also been brought down from Rs. 3746 crores in 1999-
2000 to Rs. 3202 crores in 2004-05 RE. 
(c) In a letter to the Finance Minister, the State Government has indicated 
that: 
   (i)  under the new dispensation of the Central Government not acting   as 
an intermediary for lending to States, the Central Governmen. would 
released only the grant portion of Ce ntral assistance for the State Plan 
and it would be extremely difficult for a fiscally stressed State like 
Orissa to raise market borrowing of such a magnitude. 
(ii)  release of States' share in Central taxes in monthly instalments based 
on the latest data on actual tax collection would create difficulties in 
day to day management of the ways and means position of the State 
and hamper implementation of anti-poverty programmes and 
infrastructure development since the process of collecting actual data 
will take some time. 
(d) In accordance, with the decision taken by Governme nt of India to 
implement the recommendations of the Twelfth Finance Commission 
(TFC) relating to reschedulement of Central loans to States, reduction of 
interest rate on Central loans and write -off of debt outstanding of States 
to the Central Government, guidelines have been issued to States by 
Finance Ministry for preparing a fiscal correction path and drafting fiscal 
responsibility legislation as prescribed by the TFC. Orissa has enacted a 
Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act which has come into 
force from 14th June, 2005 targeting elimination of the revenue deficit 
and reducing the fiscal deficit to 3% by 2008-09. The Twelfth Finance 
Commission has estimated the debt relief that could be available to Orissa 
from 2005-08 to 2009-2010 at Rs. 1008.43 crores in terms of lower 
interest payment and Rs. 872.85 crores in terms of principal repayments.

334. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of AGRO AND 
RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state:- 
(a) the details of Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate Scheme (ISECS) 
and Product Development Design Intervention and Packaging Scheme 
(PDDIPS) implemented by Government; 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2005] 
(b) the details of funds allocated to States under these Schemes during the 
last three years, State-wise; 
(c) whether Government propose to set up a fund with an initial amount of 
Rs. 100 crore for the regeneration of traditional industries; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHABIR PRASAD): (a) Under the Intere st Subsidy Eligibility Certificate 
(ISEC) Scheme, implemented by the Khadi and Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC), loans at the concessional rate of interest of 4 per cent 
per annum for assessed requirement of capital expenditure and working 
capital are made available by banks to registered institutions producing khadi 
and polyvastra items. The difference between the actual interest rate of the 
bank and 4 per cent is paid by the Central Government through KVIC to the 
lending bank. The Product Development Design Intervention and Packaging 
(PRODIP) Scheme aims at assisting product quality improvement, 
introduction of new designs, marketing and packaging of khadi and village 
industry products. Under this Scheme, assistance is limited to (i) Rs. 2 lakh 
per project per year or 75 per cent of the project cost, whichever is lower, in 
cases of eligible institutional entities and (ii) Rs. 1 lakh per project per year or 
75 per cent of the project cost, whiche ver is lower, in cases of eligible 
individual entrepreneurial units. 
(b) The State/Union Territory (UT)-wise details of Interest Subsidy 
Eligibility Certificates issued by the KVIC and actual availment thereof 
during the last three years are given in Statements-I, II and III (See below). 
Since implementation of the PRODIP scheme started in 2003-04 only, the 
details of funds allocated to the States/UTs for the year 2003-04 and 2004-05 
are given in Statement-IV enclosed. 
(c) and (d) In keeping with the declaration in the National Common 
Minimum Programme and the annoucemen t in the July 2004 budget speech 
of Finance Minister, a draft scheme titled the "Scheme of Fund for 
Regeneration of Traditional Industries" (SFURTI), covering traditional 
industries like coir, khadi and village in dustries, has been prepared. The draft 
Scheme, with projected commencement during 2005-06, is based on a 
"cluster approach" and has been circ ulated to the Central Ministries/ 
Departments concerned for their comments, prior to final approval.

Coal shortage 
347. SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many powe r plants are facing shortage of 
feedstock of coal; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government have approved the import of 12 million tonnes of 
thermal coal this year; and 
(d) the steps being taken by Government to overcome the shortage of 
feedstock and also to launch the domestic production of coal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYANA RAO): (a) Central Electricity Authority has reported 
that as on 19.7.2005, out of the 75 thermal power stations of the country, 13 
were having coal stock for less than seven days consumption. 
(b) The reasons for which coal stock at power house end gets depleted 
to critical level are:- 
1. Perennial unloading constraints resulting in congestion in the rail 
movement, which in turn forces Railways to impose restriction in 
movement or rakes till congestion is cleared. 
2. Delayed release of payment by power plants for coal value as well as 
railway freight often leading to regulation in movement of coal. 
3. Constraints in transport logistics coming in the way of movement of 
coal resulting in lopsided distribution of available coal amongst power 
stations. 
4. Power stations often consuming coal more than the allocated quantity 
given by Standing Linkage Committee (Short-term). 
 
(c) Ministry of Power has directed 13 power utilities to import 13.45 
million tonnes of coal during 2005-06. 
(d) in view of the increased demand of coal by power utilities to meet the 
requirement of improved Plant Load Factor and capacity addition, import of 
coal is contemplated, in addition, an inter-ministerial sub-group

is regularly monitoring movement of coal to power utilities so that 
optimisation of available coal and transport logistics are ensured to reduce the 
number of power stations under criti cal category at minimum level. The 
monthly coal allocations to power stations by Standing Linkage Committee is 
being reviewed on quarterly basis and suitable changes are made in 
allocations keeping in view the need of the particular power station. 
Movement of coal to power stations is also periodically reviewed at the level

Statement 
Increase in FDI Ceiling to 74 per cent In Telecom Sector 
The Union Cabinet on 02.02.2005 approved a proposal to enhance 
composite foreign holding in Telecom Sector to 74 per cent. With this 
decision, the current FDI ceiling in the Telecom Sect or in certain services 
such as Basic, Cellular, Unified Acce ss services, National/International Long 
Distance, V-SAT, Public Mobile Radio Trunked Services (PMRTS), Global 
Mobile Personal Communications Services (GMPCS) and other value added 
services, has been increased from 49 per cent to 74 per cent. 
The total composite foreign holding including but not limited to 
investments by Foreign Institutional Investors (Flls), Non-Resident Indians 
(NRIs), Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs), American Depository 
Receipts (ADRs), Global Deposito ry Receipts (GDRs), convertible 
preference shares, proportionate foreign investment in Indian 
promoters/investment companies including their holding companies, etc., will 
not exceed 74 per cent. Thus, 74 per cent foreign investment can be made 
directly or indirectly in the operating company or through a holding company. 
Hence, the remaining 26 per cent will be owned by resident Indian citizens or 
an Indian Company (i.e. foreign direct investment does not exceed 49 per 
cent and the management is with the In dian owners). It is clarified that 
proportionate foreign component of such an Indian Company will also be 
counted towards the ceiling of 74% . The licensee 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2005] 
will be required to disclose the status of such foreign holding and certify that 
the foreign investment is within the ceiling of 74% on a half yearly basis. 
While enhancing the FDI ceiling, certain conditions have been put in 
place to safeguard the national interest. The salient conditions are: 
(a) The majority directors on the Board including Chairman, Managing 
Director and CEO shall be resident Indian citizens. The Share Holder 
Agreements (SHA) shall specifically incorporate this condition and 
also envisage the conditions of adherence to Licence Agreement. 
(b) In order to ensure that at least one serious resident Indian promoter 
subscribes reasonable amount of the resident Indian shareholding, such 
resident Indian promoter shall hold at least 10 per cent equity of the 
licensee company. 
(c) Chief Technical Officer (CTO)/ Chief Finance Officer (CFO) should be 
resident Indian citizens. The Licenso r/DoT shall also be empowered to 
notify any key positions to be held by resident Indian citizens. 
(d) No traffic ( mobile and landline) from subscribers within India to 
subscribers within India shall be hauled to any place outside India. 
(e) The Company shall not transfer the following to any person/place 
outside India: 
(i) any accounting information relating to subscribers (except for 
roaming/billing) (note: it does not restrict a statutorily required 
disclosure of financial nature); 
(ii) user information (except pertaining to foreign subscribers using 
Indian Operator's network while roaming); and 
(iii) details of their infrastructure/network diagram except to telecom 
equipment suppliers/manufacturers who undertake the 
installation, commissioning etc. of the infrastructure of the 
licensee company on signing of non-disclosure agreement. 
These conditions shall also be made applicable to the companies operating 
telecom service (s) with existing FDI ceiling of 49 per cent. With the above 
dispensation, the present provisions in FDI policy for investment company 
will no longer be applicable for Telecom Sector as

indirect foreign investment in the licensee company will also be counted 
towards sectoral cap of 74 per cent. 
In case of not adhering to licence conditions now being imposed for 
addressing security concerns, the licence (s) granted to the company shall be 
deemed as cancelled and the licenso r shall have the right encash the 
performance bank guarantees and the licensor shall not be liable for loss of 
any kind.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (c) Since November 1, 2004, 
Australia has initiated a trial of an electronic lodgement service (e-Visa). The 
new visa regulations now introduce Assessment Levels or ALs (depending on 
country and sector), which determine requirements for financial ability 
(abiiity to meet tuition and living costs), English language proficiency 
conditions and other criteria set against the Assessment Level (AL) of the 
country of citizenship. Coun tries are divided into Assessment levels 1—4. in

Higher evidentiaiy requirements have to be met for countries falling into AL 
3-4 and lower evidentiary standards for AL 1-2. The e-Visa has been initiated

countries. 
There are currently 3 coun tries participating in the trial—India, China and 
Thailand. The trail involves 26 Indian education agencies (with 98 of their 
staff) who nave signed an agreement with  Australia to use the e-Visa system. 
So far around 1800 e-Visa applications have been lodged by these agents on 
behalf of students. Australia has provided additional training to the education 
agents in this regard and they receive regular feedback on their performance. 
When an application is e-lodged, it is processed by Australia's Adelaide 
Students Processing Centre. The staff at the Adelaide processing centre 
provides an e-mail service to ag ents in respect of any outstanding 
documentation and the visa decision. Students must still obtain a visa label 
from the Australian High Commission in Delhi before they travel. The 
Australian High Commission in Delh i also assists in managing the 
arrangements with the agents. 
As part of their access agreement to e-Visa, agents must sign a code of 
conduct and agree to terms and conditions that apply for the lodgement of the 
applications. Agents can be checked  and audited in respect of their 
applications to ensure that they do not engage in fraudulent practices.

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) The scientists at 
Integrated Coastal Marine Areal Mana gement (ICMAM) Project Directorate 
of Department of Ocean Development (DOD) have measured the run-up 
levels (maximum land elevation up to which sea water reached) and 
inundation limits (horizontal distances from the coast upto which sea water 
reached) during the Tsunami that occu rred on 26th December, 2004. The run 
up levels are useful in determining the safe locations for human settlement 
along the coast and also to validate models used in prediction of inundation of 
sea water on the land during Tsunami that may occur in future. The run up 
levels have been measured at a few locations in Andaman, Nicobar, Great 
Nicobar, Nagapattnam and Chennai coas t. The data collected has indicated 
maximum run up levels of 7 m in Car Nicobar, 4.4.m in Nagapattnam and 
3.5m in Chennai. The inundation limits varied from 45m to 1.2 km along 
Andaman, Nicobar and Tamil Nadu coasts. 
(c) and (d) The run up data has indicated the vulnerability of low lying 
areas to tsunami waves. It has been proposed to set up a Tsunami and Storm 
Surge Early Warning System with the following components. 
* Strengthening of the existing seismologicai network to indicate in near 
real time occurrence of tsunamigenic earthquakes. 
* Installation of tsunami warning sensors close to the ocean bottom at 
appropriate locales in the Indian Ocean with real time connectivity. 
* Tide gauge and data buoys networking. 
* Modelling of the inundations scenarios for the entire coast. 
* The establishment of a centre for collection of information analysis and 
generating status advisories.

of-the-art and world class facilities would be ready by 2008; 
(b) if so, the location of the third station and the details of how it proposes 
to function; and 
(c) the details of work done by the previous two stations in Antarctica? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) No, Sir. However, a 
site near latitude 69° South and longitude 76° East has been identified for 
setting up of third Indian Antarctic Station. Preliminary surveys on 
environmental parameters as mandated under the Environmental Protocol of 
the Antarctic Treaty and also from logistics and scientific considerations, 
have been carried out during the last two summer expeditions. Further studies 
and surveys are being planned to develop a detailed plan proposal for getting 
necessary clearances as per the Protocol for the new station. 
(c) The 'Dakshin Gangotri' station, which was established in the Antarctic 
summer of 1983/1984 outlived its life by 1988 and the present research 
station' 'Maitri' was made operational in 1989. Since 1981 research work is 
being carried out in the fields of Atmospheric Science, Biology and Human 
Physiology, Environmental Sciences, Earth Sciences and Glaciology, Global 
Climate Change and Engineering and Communication. 
At Maitri, eight permanent observatories have been established, which are 
providing continuous data on weather, geomagnetism, seismicity, plate 
movement, Very Low Frequency propagation, communication, 
environmental and cold acclimatization. 
So far 24 expeditions have gone to Antarctica in which more than 700 
scientists, belonging to over 50 national level institutes and organizations 
have participated. A vast array of scientific and technological information has 
been collected in addition to publicatio n of sixteen technical reports, several 
books, map and one atlas on Antarctic sea ice and more than 300 scientific 
papers. About 45 Ph. Ds have been awarded on the research work carried out 
in Antarctica.

SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: A major fire accident occurred on Mumbai 
High North (MHN) processing platform at 4.05 P.M. on 27. 7.2005 resulting in 
the loss of the facility. The accident took place when ONGC's multipurpose 
support vessel "Samudra Suraksha", under SGI operation, was engaged in a 
medicai evacuation operation. According to available information, the MSV 
lost control, drifted, and collided with the platform causing a major fire which 
also engulfed the MSV. 
Given the intensity of the fire and consequent damage the platform was 
abandoned according to a weli-rehearsed abandonment drill used in offshore 
operations, Similarly, personnel from the MSV were evacuated, except for 6 
divers who are now undergoing decompression and are expected to survive. 
Personnel on board the chartered drilling rig in NC Yester deployed in the 
area were also evacuated. The MHN platform was totally lost in less than 2 
hours along with a Pawan hans helicopter positioned on it. ONGC support 
and supply vessels and three chartered helicopters were quickly mobilized for 
search and rescue operations. Indian Navy and Coast guards provided 
prompt assistance by deploying ships and aircrafts. 
A total of 384 personnel had to abandon the affected platform and the two 
vessels. Of them, 351 have been rescued in addition to the 6 divers who are 
undergoing decompression. 
The injured persons were provided first aid by doctors and paramedics 
immediately on rescue. 129 of t hose rescued are reaching Mumbai docks 
today in the morning. The remaining rescued personnel are expected to reach 
Mumbai by last evening. The search for missing persons is continuing. 
So far, 10 personnel are confirmed dead. These include 6 from ONGC and 
1 each from the MSV and NC Yester. Two bodies are yet to be identified. On 
behalf of the nation, I extend my deepes t sympathies to be bereaved families. 
Their rehabilitation will be our duty. 
In spite of the severe destruction caused by floods and rains in Mumbai, all 
possible resources for rescue and relief were mobilized immediately.

completely grounded because of the fl ood situation. An emergency control 
centre was set up immediately to mana ge the response effectively. CMD, 
ONGC and other officers of ONGC have already reached Mumbai on 28th 
early morning by the first civilian flight to land on the opening of Mumbai 
airport. Shri Mani Shankar Aiyar, the Minister in-charge is leaving for Mumbai

Though the loss of the platform would immediately impact 110,000 barrels 
per day of crude production, it is expect ed that 70 per cent of this production 
would be restored over the next 4 weeks. The platform was insured for US$ 
195 million and the MSV for US$ 60 million under ONGC's offshore package 
insurance policy. 
CMD, ONGC has constituted an internal  enquiry committee to go into the 
causes of this tragic accident with the help of outside experts. 
I would like to draw the attention of the House to the outstanding success

Guards who have mounted a remarkab ly rapid and extremely successful 
search and rescue operation. My thanks are also due to Cairn Energy and 
British Gas who have offered their helicopters for the rescue operations.

*84.SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of AIDS/HIV affected patients, State-wise in the year 2000; 
(b) the number of new cases registered, year-wise thereafter till 31st May, 
2005; 
(c) the details of special drive undertaken, if any, for ascertaining their numbers 
as well as identifying the affected persons who might be avoiding to come to 
Government health centres; 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
(d) the details of NGOs engaged in combating AIDS; 
(e) the funds allocated to each, year-wise since 2000-2001; 
(f) whether a phenomenal change in th e number of HIV/AIDS affected 
persons was observed in the recent past; and 
(g) if so, what could it be attributed to? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) and (b) A st atement indicating State-wise 
number of AIDS/HIV affected patients year-wise during the year 2000 and 
number of new cases registered year-wise, every year, till 31st May, 2005, is 
enclosed Statements I and II (see below). 
(c) As per the standard AIDS case definition adopted under the 
programme, all States/UTs are reporti ng AIDS cases on a monthly basis to 
National AIDS Control Organisation. However, as there is high under reporting 
of cases, we are relying on HIV surveillance mechanism as HIV is the first 
stage of disease. This enables us to tr ack the course of AIDS epidemic in the 
country. The National AIDS Control Organization conducts annual round of 
HIV sentinel surveillance in designated sites all over the country. The data thus 
collected is used to monitor HlV trends in various risk groups of population over 
time and in different geographical areas. This set of data is also used to work out 
estimated number of HIV infections in the c ountry on an annual basis. This 
process takes care of minimizing the participation bias by the individuals who 
might oe avoiding coming to Government Health Centres. Such bias is taken care 
by doing the surveillance activities using "unlinked anonymous" metnodology 
and consecutive sampling. This methodology has been recognized as a 
globally accepted methodology based on the guidelines issued from WHO and 
UNAIDS from time to time. 
(d) and (e) Under the National AIDS Control Programme Phase-ll, grants 
are given to NGOs through the State AI DS Control Societies for undertaking 
Targeted Interventions addressing mainly the groups at higher risk of contracting 
HIV infection and to provide care & support services for people living with 
HIV/AIDS. As on date, 922 NGOs are implementing 965 Targeted Intervention 
projects among High Risk Groups (HRGs) such as Commercial Sex Workers 
(CSWs), Injecting Drug Users (IDUs), Men who have sex with men (MSM), 
Migrant Workers and Street Children 
30

[29 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
etc. and 58 NGOs are running 60 Community Care Centres (CCCs) across 
the country. The Funding of NGOs has been decentralized to the respective 
State AIDS Control Societies (SACS) for which detailed operational and 
costing guidelines have been provided to them. Based on annual action 
discussions with the States, the funds are released to respective State AIDS 
Control Societies for providing financial assistance to NGOs implementing the 
Targeted Interventions and Community Care Centres. A statement indicating the 
allocation of funds for NGOs in annual action pain of State AIDS Control Societies 
(SACS) to undertake Targeted Interventions and Community Care Centres from 
2000-01 to 2004-05 is enclosed Statement-Ill (see below). However, the 
details of NGOs engaged and funds released to each of these NGOs year-wise 
since 2000-01 are being collected and will be laid on the Table of the House. 
(f) and (g) Based on the data received form annual round of HIV 
sentinel surveillance, it is estimated that there are 5.134 million HIV 
infections in the country in 2004, as compared to 5.106 million infections in 
2003 and 4.58 million in 2002. There is no spurt in the number of cases in the 
country. There are States like Tamil Nadu where HIV infection has shown signs 
of sero-stabilisation, while in some States, HIV prevalence has increased. It 
has been observed that within the States there are pockets of very high HIV 
prevalence across the country.

Effect of Forest Conservation Act, 1980 on developmental works 
†*89.   SHRI SURENDRA LATH: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Forest Conservation Act, 1980 is the main 
hurdle in implementation of Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana and other 
developmental work particularly in Orissa; 
(b) if so, the number of cases seeking permission for construction of 
roads on the forest land falling enroute and other development works under the 
scheme forwarded by the State Government during last three years alongwith 
the number of cases cleared and pending so far; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government for a permanent solution to the 
problem? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) to (c) No, Sir. Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, is a regulatory and not 
a prohibitory Act. It has the enabling provisions for the Central Government to 
grant permission for non-forestry use of forest land for developmental 
purposes. Proposals for forestry clearance for construction of roads under Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) are dealt 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi,   
41 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2005] 
on priority basis, in respect of all the States/Union Territories including the 
State of Orissa. Further, for up-gradation of roads constructed in forest areas 
prior to 1980, from 'Kutchcha to Pucca' , without widening , prior permission 
under this Act is not required. Guidelin es have already been issued by the 
Ministry of Environment and Forest on 30th April 2005 in this regard. 
However, if any such project falls in a National Park/ Sanctuary, prior 
permission of National Board of wildlife (NBWL) and the Supreme Court, is 
essential. In so far as other developmental works are concerned, Central 
Government has already granted general approval under this Act on 3rd January 
2005, for infrastructure development projects upto 1.0 hectares, to be 
implemented by Government Departments, like school, dispensary/hospital, 
electric lines, drinking water, rain water harvesting structure minor irrigation 
canal, non-conventional sources of energy, skill upgradation/vocational training 
centre, power sub-stations etc. 
During last three years (01-07-2002 to 01-07-2005), Government of 
Orissa has submitted a total of 106 development project proposals including 
12 for construction of roads (2 under PMGSY). Out of total proposals 
received, 75 projects including 11 for construction of roads (2 under PMGSY), 
have been approved by the Central Government on merit and ecological 
considerations. Only 5 cases of Orissa are under various stages of consideration 
of the Central Government. None of these case pertain to construction of roads. 
Remaining 26 cases have either been rejected for valid reasons, or returned to 
the State Government due to incomplete information. No proposal for 
construction of roads on forest lands in Orissa including construction under 
PMGSY, is pending with the Central Government.
